parts_read: The whole extracted text of the 52-page PDF: front matter, abstract, keywords, table of contents, lists of tables and figures (all captions), Sec. 1 (introduction and literature review, Tables 1 and 2), Sec. 2.1 (photogrammetry, collinearity, epipolar geometry, printed pp. 9 to 12), Sec. 2.2 (layout, control and data acquisition, processing flowchart, pp. 12 to 15), Sec. 2.3 (OpenPTV methodology, spatial calibration, tracking efficiency and trajectory recombination, Table 3, pp. 15 to 19), Sec. 2.4 (visual hull sizing and resolution calibration, pp. 19 to 22), Sec. 3 (rotating punk stick and falling sphere validations, pp. 22 to 27), Sec. 4 (NFRL firebrand shower: layout, tracking, CPC/PNF, firebrand rose, comparison with a prescribed fire, sizing, pp. 27 to 34), Sec. 5 Final Remarks (pp. 35 to 36), Sec. 6 Conclusion (p. 37), the reference list, and Appendix A Table A1 (p. 44). Page numbers are the printed page numbers. Figures were NOT viewed as images; only their captions and the body text were read, so values that exist only in plotted curves (for example the per-timestep tracked/new/lost counts in Fig. 8 or the full PNF time series in Fig. 22) were not extracted. Symbol-font characters lost by pdftotext were checked in the plain-mode output (theta = polar, phi = azimuth, approximately-equal signs).

relevant_methods.details: Four consumer-grade compact cameras (Sony DSC-RX10 M3, about 20.1 Mpx) mounted at both ends of two horizontal rails (2.03 m long) whose upper faces are at 0.356 m and 1.880 m height, on a mobile stand so the system can be moved without performing additional calibrations. Cameras aimed with tripod heads so image centers closely coincide with a target point T (0 m, 1.041 m, 0 m) on which focus is set; each camera carries a collimated laser diode and all beams intersect at T, which is also used at the start of each experiment to detect unwanted changes of camera orientation. Minimum focal length (f = 8.8 mm), largest aperture (f/2.4). Control volume is the intersection of the fields of view, corrected for small volumes not accounted for during spatial calibration, estimated at about 1.91 m3 (Table 1 rounds it to 2 m3). Working distance about 1.2 m to 2.8 m (Table 2). No illumination is used; tracers are glowing firebrands (Table 1).
relevant_methods.location: Sec. 2.2.1, pp. 12 to 13, Fig. 5; Table 1 last row p. 4; Table 2 last row p. 7

relevant_methods.details: HD video (1920x1080 px) at a nominal 120 fps. Near-field triggering by IR remote receivers; long-range triggering via a custom RF control hub (433.92 MHz) that also triggers a sync laser. Streams are synchronized post-acquisition on the disappearance of a small laser dot, manually operated and visible from all cameras. Synchronization verified by imaging a millisecond-precision digital counter; error found to be within the time lapse between two consecutive frames, up to the highest available frame rate (960 fps). The frame rate actually used for tracking in the Sec. 4 shower is not stated; Fig. 22 says a 30-timestep window is about 1 s, which implies (my inference) roughly 30 timesteps per second after temporal downsampling, not 120.
relevant_methods.location: Sec. 2.2.2, pp. 13 to 14; Fig. 22 caption p. 30

relevant_methods.details: Frames are extracted unaltered from video (32-bit color) with commercial software, then synchronized and converted to 8-bit grayscale in an in-house MATLAB code, with optional temporal downsampling to reduce tracking cost when motion is too highly resolved. Grayscale sequences plus spatial calibration go to OpenPTV; an in-house FORTRAN code builds per-particle 'ID I' files (frame number, time step, 3D object coordinates, 2D coordinates in all four views, velocity from previous and current positions, distance D and local resolution R*). Color sequences are used later for sizing.

Firebrand 2D image coordinates are found with a pixel-intensity-weighted centroid operator inside OpenPTV. The text gives no detection threshold values, no background subtraction or background model, and no size limits for detection. The tracking-efficiency monitoring described below is said to provide, 'to some extent', guidance for choosing detection and tracking parameters. The uncertainty table assumes uniform pixel intensity across silhouettes (no bias in centroid detection). For sizing only, particle boundaries are found by a multi-step boundary detection that follows an unsupervised threshold selection method (Otsu 1979, ref. [56]) and needs no user input.

3D V-shaped target with 76 dots of known 3D coordinates, all visible from the four viewpoints, processed by spatial resection to get internal and external orientation of each camera. A verification test is systematically performed after calibration by re-processing the original target images and comparing known and measured target point positions; the expanded uncertainty in position is typically on the order of plus or minus 1.5 mm in all directions. Because the verification re-uses the calibration target images, this is an in-sample residual, not an independent test on separate points.
relevant_methods.location: Sec. 2.3.2, p. 16, Fig. 7; Table A1 p. 44

relevant_methods.details: Correspondence across views by epipolar line intersection: the search for a match in view 2 is restricted to a narrow band around the epipolar line, limited in length by the known depth of the object space and with a transverse tolerance; intersecting the search bands from the 3rd and 4th views establishes the correspondence unambiguously, and 3D coordinates are computed, for instance by least-squares adjustment of the collinearity equations. The text states that at least two images from calibrated devices with different orientations are needed to recover 3D coordinates.

Tracking by spatio-temporal particle matching using both image-space and object-space information (OpenPTV, following Maas et al. and Willneff). No tracking parameter values (search radii, acceleration limits) are given in the text. Only particles inside the control volume are tracked; firebrands visible in camera 4 near the generator exit that have not yet entered the control volume are not tracked.

The authors argue the quad-view setup suits firebrands because visibility can vary strongly with imaging angle (for example background interference). Particle #145 has an incomplete trajectory in the image plane of camera 1, but its 3D trajectory is still reconstructed because the other image planes have the information.

Qualitative check: at each timestep count all particles located in 3D inside a test volume chosen well inside the control volume (X -600 to 600 mm, Y 600 to 1400 mm, Z -300 to 300 mm for the Sec. 4 case), split into 'tracked' (identified before and after the current timestep), 'new' (identified for the first time in the current timestep) and 'lost' (not identified beyond the current timestep). A close match between total and tracked counts indicates good tracking efficiency. The test volume is kept well within the control volume to avoid counting appearance and disappearance events near the control-volume boundaries. Described as providing, to some extent, guidance for choosing detection and tracking parameters. New and lost events are described as seldom and usually associated with the non-ideal trajectory types below.

Three non-ideal trajectory types: (1) spurious: unwanted, lasting very few time steps with very small averaged displacement, usually due to a secondary tracked object (examples given: a landed firebrand, a bright element in the background); typically filtered out prior to any tracking or sizing analysis with an operator based on the mean particle displacement, but it may remain on rare occasions if the operator is set to include very slow (small) firebrands; (2) incomplete or shortened: valid trajectory with late start or early end inside the measurement volume, missing steps possibly due to lack of visibility, processed like full trajectories; (3) broken: valid portion of a trajectory for which at least one sister portion can be found in the measurement volume, correspondences unknown a priori. The threshold value of the mean-displacement operator is NOT reported, the text does not say whether the displacement is measured in 3D object space or in image space (it is applied to the reconstructed 3D trajectories, so object space is the likely reading, but that is an inference), and no separate minimum-length rule is stated.

Fig. 21b shows a reconstructed 'slow' firebrand trajectory, presented by the authors as an example of the low-velocity ember dynamics the system resolves, that does not appear in the cumulative plot of Fig. 21a because it is filtered out by the mean displacement operator. So the displacement filter removed a trajectory the authors treat as a real slow ember from the analysed set. Sec. 2.3.3 also acknowledges the tradeoff: a spurious trajectory may remain if the operator is set to include very slow (small) firebrands. Low-velocity motion (below 0.4 m/s) of small, air-draft and lift-force sensitive embers is stated to occur in this shower. The text gives no count of how many genuine slow firebrands were removed and no count of how many spurious trajectories the filter removed.
relevant_methods.location: Fig. 21 caption p. 30; Sec. 4.2.1 p. 29; Sec. 2.3.3 p. 17

relevant_methods.details: Within a specified volume (its bounds are not reported), each early-ended (EE) trajectory gets a list of late-started (LS) candidates whose start falls in a user-specified temporal search window that directly follows the EE end and has limited duration (6 timesteps 'in the present case'). A linear best fit (ref. [55]) on the EE data points, shown in the Fig. 9 caption as the last four EE points, predicts X, Y, Z versus time across the window. The first and second LS points are compared with predictions; per the Fig. 9 caption, 'in the present case' the tolerance is plus or minus 50 mm for the first point and c times tolerance = 75 mm for the second (relaxation factor c = 1.5), so the widening is from the first to the second LS point, not a function of the gap length. EE and LS are matched if both points fall within tolerance in all directions. Motivation: otherwise each portion is attributed to a new particle, so in size distribution analyses one particle could be counted several times and sizing data from sister trajectories would not be merged. The recombination is stated to be applied for the sizing analysis of Sec. 4.2.3; the text does not say whether it was applied to the trajectories used for the CPC/PNF flux counts or to Fig. 21a. The text does not explicitly confirm that the Fig. 9 tolerance values were the exact settings of the Table 3 run, although that is the natural reading.
relevant_methods.location: Sec. 2.3.3 pp. 17 to 18, Fig. 9 caption p. 18, Table 3 p. 19

relevant_methods.method: 3D shape reconstruction (visual hull) and resolution calibration
relevant_methods.details: Per timestep, silhouettes are segmented in each of the four views (Otsu), placed at the 3D particle location, rescaled with a per-camera resolution map (mm/pixel versus distance D to the camera reference plane, from a pole carrying six 25.4 mm white spheres moved to 22 locations), wrapped in convex envelopes and projected as cones; the intersection of the four cones is the hull, sampled by random points. Hulls from all timesteps (typically about 10 models) are reoriented by PCA and their orthogonal outlines accumulated for sizing. Known nonsystematic artifact: blind volumes not carved by the silhouette projection cones can remain and artificially enlarge the hull (seen along the y axis in Sec. 3.2 and the z axis in Sec. 4.2.3).
relevant_methods.location: Sec. 2.4 pp. 19 to 22, Figs. 10 to 12; Sec. 3.2 pp. 25 to 26; Sec. 4.2.3 p. 33

relevant_methods.details: Rotating lit punk stick (53.5 mm exposed length, about 3.6 mm thick) on a metallic arm (397 mm axis-to-axis) driven by a DC gear motor; the glowing lit end serves as a model firebrand. Recorded at 120 Hz over two complete revolutions, downsampled to 12 Hz (136 data points), compared with the trajectory predicted from the known layout (prediction uncertainty likely about plus or minus 5 mm in all directions). This is a single known glowing object; it tests 3D position and velocity accuracy, not detection precision, false positives or fragmentation.

relevant_methods.method: Exact controlled case behind the trajectory statistics
relevant_methods.details: Artificial firebrand shower at the NIST National Fire Research Laboratory (NFRL): emberometer placed downstream of a firebrand generator (centrifugal blower Cincinnati Fan PB-9 in line with 149 mm I.D. stainless steel duct), operated to give showers whose particle number densities are visually consistent with field observations. Fuel: 350 g plus or minus 1 g of Douglas fir cuboids (7.8 mm, 8.1 mm, 12.9 mm, plus or minus 0.4 mm), moisture below 6 %. Blower at 5 Hz with two propane torches for 45 s, then propane stopped and blower at 20 Hz; a large flame settled at the outlet and disappeared after about 48 s; first firebrands about 16 s after flame onset, generation for about 74 s. Analysis restricted to a 35 s window starting 38 s after flame onset (peak production). Most landing firebrands were collected in water pans (about 2.4 m2, starting 0.56 m downstream of the generator exit) for an independent size dataset (999 firebrands). Ambient lighting and background conditions are not described, and the text does not explicitly say whether the test was indoors (it is contrasted with an outdoor fire).

Cumulative Particle Count (CPC, particles per m2) of trajectories crossing a reference disk (center X = -150 mm, Y = 1000 mm, Z = 0 mm, radius 200 mm); Particle Number Flux (PNF, particles per m2 per s) derived from CPC over a 30-timestep window (about 1 s). 'Firebrand rose' repeats this for reference-surface orientations in 15 degree increments (polar angle theta, azimuth phi).

reported_results_with_definitions: Table 3 trajectory-type breakdown, defined as 'numbers of particle trajectory by type for the test case presented in Sec. 4 (combusting cuboids) after proceeding to trajectory recombination', percent of all trajectories (count): Spurious 0.15 % (1); Singles 85.8 % (593); Broken, successfully recombined 12.6 % (87); Broken, not recombined 1.45 % (10); Total 100 % (691). Population: the single NFRL artificial firebrand shower test (Douglas fir cuboids, 35 s peak window), four calibrated synchronized cameras, laboratory setting. The text does not say how a trajectory was judged spurious (no manual ground-truth protocol is described). It does not explicitly state whether Table 3 is counted before or after the mean-displacement filter, but the Table 3 total (691) equals the 691 trajectories plotted in Fig. 21a, from which the displacement operator had already removed at least one trajectory (the slow firebrand of Fig. 21b); this indicates Table 3 is post-filter, so the 1 spurious trajectory is a residual that survived the filter, matching the text's remark that a spurious trajectory 'might remain'. How many trajectories the filter removed is not reported. The text also does not make explicit whether the 691 total counts trajectory segments or merged trajectories. My arithmetic: broken trajectories together are 97 of 691, about 14 %; 1 of 691 is 0.145 %, printed as 0.15.

Recombination efficiency: 'the algorithm allows to recombine up to 90 % (87 out of 97 total) of all broken trajectories', same Sec. 4 combusting cuboids dataset, with a 6-timestep search window and, per the Fig. 9 caption ('in the present case'), tolerances of plus or minus 50 mm (first point) and 75 mm (second point) in 3D object space. 87 of 97 is 89.7 %. Correctness of the 87 matches was not independently verified in the text.
Synchronization error: within the time lapse between two consecutive frames, up to the highest available frame rate (960 fps); verified by imaging a millisecond-precision digital counter.

3D position uncertainty: typically on the order of plus or minus 1.5 mm in all directions (expanded uncertainty; Sec. 1.4 sets k = 2, Table A1 says 95 % confidence or greater), estimated during the spatial calibration procedure by re-processing the original 76-dot target images (in-sample); Table A1 notes it assumes uniform pixel intensity across particle silhouettes.

Rotating punk stick tracking validation (136 points, 12 Hz after downsampling from 120 Hz, two revolutions): measured radius 396.2 mm plus or minus 2.3 mm versus predicted 396.9 mm; measured height 1526.9 mm plus or minus 3.7 mm versus predicted 1523.3 mm; measured mean velocity 44.3 cm/s plus or minus 1.9 cm/s versus predicted 44.3 cm/s (predicted average over two turns).

Number of reconstructed trajectories in the shower test: 691 3D trajectories (Fig. 21a, after the mean-displacement filter). The Conclusion describes this as the motions of nearly 700 firebrands reconstructed over 35 s, but by Table 3 the 691 includes 1 spurious trajectory and 97 broken trajectory pieces (87 of which were recombined with sister pieces), so it is not a count of distinct firebrands.

Range of resolved dynamics in the shower test: low-velocity motion below 0.4 m/s of small embers and projectile-like motion above 4 m/s of gravity-driven embers (Sec. 4.2.1); Conclusion: velocities from tens of cm/s to several m/s.

CPC on the reference disk (center -150, 1000, 0 mm; radius 200 mm): total close to 1281 particles per m2 over the test period. PNF peaks at 111.3 particles per m2 per s at t = 9 s, most values in 25 to 65 particles per m2 per s (30-timestep derivation window, about 1 s).

Firebrand rose (15 degree increments, same disk center): highest total CPC 1329 particles per m2 for polar 15 degrees and azimuth 225 to 285 degrees, with PNF above 40 particles per m2 per s for cumulated periods exceeding a third of the test duration; for a vertical surface parallel to the generator exit (polar 90, azimuth 270 degrees) total CPC drops to about 573 particles per m2 with virtually no time above 40.

Comparison with a prescribed fire (Thomas et al., ref. [29]): highest flux there estimated at most 7 particles per m2 per s using peak-collection durations of 67 s to 122 s (with the total collected count, hence called conservative); the present test, extrapolated to a ground-facing surface (polar 0, azimuth 0) at 120 mm height, gives a time-averaged PNF slightly higher than 24 particles per m2 per s, more than 3 times that.

Table A1 expanded uncertainties (95 % or greater): particle speed plus or minus 1 % (most common Sec. 4 trajectories, major contribution from positioning uncertainty); CPC and PNF minus 0 %, plus 4 %, with the major contribution from broken trajectories, assuming they occur randomly in space and time, and possibly different if conditions change (for example tracking efficiency); PNF value valid for a fixed temporal derivation window; particle size plus or minus 2 mm (x and y axes) and minus 5 mm, plus 0 mm (z axis) for the Fig. 24a cuboid measurements.

Sizing validation with 110 non-combusting quasi-spherical particles (classes 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 mm): x and z sizes agree relatively well with known diameters (with a shift toward smaller classes attributed to nonuniform illumination biasing contours about 1 pixel inward); some y sizes fall well beyond the largest sphere diameter because of a visual hull artifact. The authors state that, based on the mean of the x, y, z sizes, 'an exact sphere size classification can be achieved' (Fig. 17 histogram comparison; no per-particle classification accuracy figure is given). Resolution about 1.6 mm per pixel at the back of the control volume.

Shower sizing versus 999 water-collected firebrands: distributions agree very well in 1 mm classes for the longest (y) dimension and the airborne x dimension (compared with collected z); airborne z is overestimated (visual hull artifact). The number of airborne firebrands sized is not stated.

Camera relocation study (fictitious 25.4 mm sphere, computed reconstruction): with camera 4 moved out of plane, most data points fall below a 15 % volume overestimation level, a marked improvement over the original position.
must_not_transfer: The 0.15 % (1 of 691) spurious-trajectory figure must not be quoted as a false-positive rate, precision, or expected spurious rate for wfglink. It comes from one laboratory firebrand-generator test at NIST NFRL with four calibrated, synchronized cameras, where (by the method described, my inference) a spurious detection also had to find epipolar correspondences in other views to become a 3D trajectory. The text gives no labeling protocol for deciding what was spurious, and the evidence indicates the count is a residual after a mean-displacement filter whose threshold and removal count are not reported.

The 90 % recombination figure (87 of 97) and its parameters (6-timestep window, linear fit on the last 4 points, plus or minus 50 mm and 75 mm tolerances, relaxation 1.5) are defined in metric 3D object space at their unstated effective processing rate (about 30 timesteps per second by inference from Fig. 22). They must not be copied as pixel tolerances or frame counts, or presented as an expected wfglink fragmentation-repair rate.

No numeric threshold for the mean-displacement filter exists in the text, so none may be cited. The text does not state the space or units of the operator; since it is applied to reconstructed 3D trajectories it likely uses 3D displacement (inference). In any case a single camera cannot tell a slow near ember from a fast far one or from a static bright spot at an unknown depth, so the same rule is weaker in pixel space.

The text does not show that displacement filtering is safe for genuine embers. The evidence points the other way: it removed a trajectory the authors present as a real slow firebrand (Fig. 21b), and Sec. 2.3.3 notes that setting the operator to keep very slow firebrands can let spurious trajectories remain. Do not claim the filter has negligible recall cost; no count of removed genuine firebrands is given.

Velocity values (below 0.4 m/s to above 4 m/s, 44.3 cm/s), position uncertainty (plus or minus 1.5 mm), speed uncertainty (plus or minus 1 %), and CPC/PNF uncertainty (minus 0, plus 4 %) all depend on multi-camera calibration and triangulation and do not transfer to a single uncalibrated RGB camera.

Flux metrics (CPC 1281 or 1329 particles per m2, PNF 111.3 peak, firebrand rose, the 3x comparison with a prescribed fire) are specific to that shower, reference surface, and 3D geometry. wfglink counts are image-plane track counts and must not be expressed or compared in particles per m2 or per m2 per s.

Do not cite 691 trajectories or 'nearly 700 firebrands' as a distinct-ember count or as a counting-accuracy benchmark; it includes a spurious trajectory and broken pieces, and the text does not say whether recombination was applied before the flux counts.

Size results, visual hull accuracy, and resolution maps require four views and a resolution calibration in mm. A single camera cannot give metric ember size; do not cite their sizing accuracy for wfglink blob sizes.

The robustness argument (Particle #145 recovered from other views when one view lost it) is a multi-view property. A single camera has no redundant view, so missing detections in wfglink become fragmentation or misses.
The tracking-efficiency check uses a 3D test volume inside a 3D control volume. Its qualitative 'good tracking efficiency' conclusion is about their system and test only, not a benchmark for wfglink.
The punk-stick validation tracks one known glowing object; it says nothing about detection precision, false positives, or fragmentation and must not be cited as evidence for any of those.

Do not describe the emberometer results as field-validated wildfire data. The tracking statistics come from a controlled NFRL lab shower; field deployability is a design goal and outdoor emberometer results are not reported in this note (the outdoor comparison uses another study's ground-collection data). Ambient lighting, background, and whether the test was indoors are not described, so do not claim a dark, clean, or indoor scene either way.
Their pipeline converts frames to 8-bit grayscale for detection and tracking. The paper provides no evidence about color cues for ember verification; do not cite it as support for any RGB color rule.
The listed sources of spurious tracks (landed firebrand, bright background element) are examples only; no per-source statistics are given.
Laser-dot synchronization and laser-beam orientation checks are multi-camera procedures; their sub-frame synchronization result has no meaning for a single camera.
proposed_adaptations: Proposed adaptation: use the paper's track taxonomy (spurious, incomplete, broken, single) as audit labels for wfglink tracks on its own labeled clips, and report a Table 3 style breakdown with counts, a written labeling protocol, and an explicit statement of whether it is measured before or after verifier filtering, plus how many tracks each filter removed.

Proposed adaptation: add a low-displacement rule to the rules stage (net or mean displacement over the first N frames), but treat it as a feature or soft score for the temporal classifier rather than a hard reject, because the paper shows such a filter removed a slow firebrand trajectory. Report the recall cost on labeled slow embers alongside the precision gain. Any threshold must be tuned on wfglink data in pixels and could be normalized by blob size since depth is unknown.

Proposed adaptation: since the paper names landed firebrands and bright background elements as typical sources of spurious tracks, add a static bright-spot memory (per-location accumulator of long-lived, near-stationary detections) so candidates that sit on known static bright locations are rejected or down-weighted; this is a single-camera substitute for the cross-view check they had.

Proposed adaptation: broken-track recombination before counting so one ember is not counted twice. Link an early-ended track to a late-started track within a short window using linear extrapolation of the last few image positions. Their method uses a fixed tolerance for the first matched point and a 1.5x wider tolerance for the second; a tolerance that grows with gap length would be a wfglink design choice, not something the paper did. To stay causal, delay the count of an ended track by the window length or merge before a count is committed. Window and pixel tolerances must be tuned on wfglink data.

Proposed adaptation: per-frame tracked, new and lost counts inside an inner image region away from frame borders, used as a health monitor for tracker fragmentation and flicker; spikes in new or lost tracks without matching entry or exit events flag problems.

Proposed adaptation: count only tracks that are accepted inside an inner counting region away from image borders, by analogy with their test volume kept well inside the control volume for efficiency monitoring (their own counts use crossings of a reference disk in the core flow), so border entry and exit are not confused with track starts and ends.

Proposed adaptation: use an intensity-weighted centroid for sub-pixel blob positions, and Otsu thresholding inside a candidate patch to get a silhouette for simple shape features fed to the small patch classifier (in the paper Otsu is used only for sizing silhouettes, not detection).

Proposed adaptation: replace the missing cross-view evidence with weaker temporal evidence: residual of a short linear or quadratic fit of the track, direction consistency, and smooth speed. Document clearly that this cannot recover depth, metric speed or metric size.

Proposed adaptation: build a controlled positive test like their rotating punk stick (a lit incense or punk stick on a motor arm with known period) filmed by the single camera, to check that the tracker gives one unbroken track per revolution, measure fragmentation, and confirm slow-moving genuine glows are not rejected by the displacement rule (the paper itself used this rig only for position and velocity accuracy).

Proposed adaptation: analog of their laser orientation check: compare against a reference frame or estimate global motion at the start of each clip and during runs, flagging camera bumps that make static bright background spots appear to move and could create false tracks.

problems.claim: Table 3 result and must_not_transfer item 1: 'does not say whether this count is taken before or after the mean-displacement filter.'
problems.issue: Incomplete. It is true that this is not stated explicitly for Table 3, but the text gives strong evidence. Sec. 4.2.1 says 'Fig. 21a shows a cumulated plot of 691 3D trajectories reconstructed in the present case', and the Fig. 21 caption says the slow trajectory 'does not show on Fig. (a) since it is filtered out by the mean displacement operator'. Table 3 also totals 691. So the counts are very likely post-filter, and the 1 spurious trajectory is one that survived the filter, which matches 'In rare occasions, it might remain'. For a precision-first project this matters: 0.15 % is a post-filter residual, not a raw spurious rate.
problems.correction: State that Table 3 is not explicitly labelled pre- or post-filter. Its total (691) equals the Fig. 21a set, which had already passed the mean-displacement filter, so it is most likely post-filter, with the 1 spurious trajectory a residual. The number of trajectories the filter removed is not reported.

problems.claim: must_not_transfer item 1: 'one indoor laboratory firebrand-generator test at NIST NFRL'
problems.issue: The text never says the NFRL test was indoors. It only contrasts the test with 'an actual outdoor fire'. Table 1 lists the application as 'Indoor/Outdoor'.
problems.correction: Say 'one laboratory firebrand-generator test at NIST NFRL', and add that the text does not state whether it was indoors.

problems.claim: must_not_transfer item 3: 'Their filter also runs on metric 3D displacement'
problems.issue: Not stated. The text only says 'an operator based on the mean particle displacement'. It gives no units and does not say whether displacement is measured in object space or image space.
problems.correction: Say the space and units are not stated. Because the operator is applied to reconstructed 3D trajectories, 3D displacement is the likely reading, but that is an inference.

problems.claim: must_not_transfer item 4: 'The only evidence on that point is that it removed a genuine slow firebrand (Fig. 21b).'
problems.issue: Overstated. Sec. 2.3.3 also acknowledges the tradeoff: a spurious trajectory 'might remain if the operator is set to include very slow (small) firebrands'. Also, 'genuine' is how the authors frame it (they present the trajectory as an example of resolved slow-ember dynamics), not something verified independently.
problems.correction: Cite both pieces of evidence: Fig. 21b, and the Sec. 2.3.3 sentence about operator settings. Describe the trajectory as one 'the authors present as a real slow firebrand'.

problems.claim: Proposed adaptation 4: 'with a tolerance that grows with the gap (like their relaxation factor)'
problems.issue: This misdescribes the paper. The relaxation factor c = 1.5 widens the tolerance for the second matched LS point compared with the first (50 mm, then 75 mm). The tolerance does not depend on the gap between the EE end and the LS start.
problems.correction: Describe their method as a fixed tolerance for the first LS point and a 1.5x wider tolerance for the second. A tolerance that grows with gap length would be a wfglink design choice.

problems.claim: Recombination method and result: parameters given as the settings of the Table 3 run (linear fit on the last four points, plus or minus 50 mm and 75 mm), plus 'The recombination is stated to be applied for the sizing analysis of Sec. 4.2.3.'
problems.issue: The four-point fit and the tolerance values come from the Fig. 9 caption ('In the present case'); the body text only says the fit uses 'the EE trajectory data points'. The bounds of the 'specified volume' are not reported. The record also leaves out that the text never says whether recombination was applied to the CPC/PNF flux counts or to Fig. 21a, which matters for wfglink counting.
problems.correction: Attribute the tolerances and the four-point fit to the Fig. 9 caption. Note that tying them to the Table 3 run is the natural reading but is not explicit. Note that the volume bounds are unreported, and that recombination is stated only for sizing (Sec. 4.2.3), not for the flux counts.

problems.claim: Result: '691 3D trajectories (Fig. 21a); Conclusion describes this as nearly 700 firebrands reconstructed over 35 s.'
problems.issue: This needs a caveat. By Table 3, the 691 includes 1 spurious trajectory and 97 broken trajectory pieces, 87 of which were recombined with sister pieces. So 691 is not a count of distinct firebrands, even though the Conclusion words it that way.

relevant_methods.details: Four compact cameras (Sony DSC-RX10 M3, about 20 MP; Sect. 3 calls the rig consumer-grade electronics) at the ends of two horizontal rails, at minimum focal length (8.8 mm) and largest aperture (f/2.4). Control volume, defined as the intersection of the camera fields of view, is about 1.91 m3. Streams were synchronized after acquisition using the disappearance of a laser dot visible to all cameras. Frames are converted to grayscale for tracking, with optional downsampling to cut computation for the 3D tracking step. A data acquisition frequency of 120 fps is quoted only for the expected velocity limits (Sect. 2.1). The effective tracking frame rate used in the NFRL test is not stated. The Fig. 8 caption equates a 30 timestep window with about 1 s, which implies about 30 timesteps per second, and the text does not reconcile this with 120 fps.

OpenPTV finds firebrand 2D image coordinates with a pixel intensity-weighted centroid operator, which the paper says was 'confirmed to efficiently process glowing/hot particles'. That efficiency is not quantified.

Particle correspondences across the four views use the epipolar line intersection technique, then 3D coordinates are computed in object space. Tracking is spatio-temporal particle matching using both image-space and object-space information (details deferred to Maas 1991; Maas et al. 1993; Willneff 2003). Calibration uses a custom 3D V-shaped target with 76 white dots. The paper does not describe any separate spurious-detection or spurious-trajectory rejection step, and it does not discuss whether or how multi-view correspondence suppresses distractors. Any view that it acts as an implicit consistency filter is reviewer inference, not a statement in the paper.

The paper says that, 'although seldom', a broken trajectory 'can occur if' a firebrand's visibility becomes challenging, and gives one example (low glow against a very bright background object). It does not give a full list of causes. Dedicated algorithms predict, within a user-specified temporal window, the missing positions of firebrands whose trajectories ended early, then identify 'sister' trajectories by spatio-temporal matching in each particle image plane. The window length, prediction model and matching thresholds are not given in the main text; the paper defers to Bouvet et al. 2020 (NIST TN 2093). The stated purpose in Sect. 4.1 is 'to support the airborne firebrand sizing analysis', with avoiding counting broken tracks as independent particles given in parentheses as a second aim.

Particle image densities on the order of 4 x 10^-5 particles per pixel are 'considered' in this work. The paper says this is similar to density estimates from field work data (e.g. Filkov and Prohanov 2018), one to two orders of magnitude below large-scale PTV with controlled seeding, and two orders below densities known to promote triangulation errors (about 5 x 10^-3 ppp, Maas et al. 1993).

relevant_methods.method: Resolvability limits derived from imaging geometry
relevant_methods.details: Minimum particle size of 2 mm is a conservative estimate from the lowest spatial resolution in the control volume and a minimum particle image size of 1 pixel. The lower velocity limit (0.27 m/s) assumes a 1-pixel particle image diameter (no subpixel accuracy), a 1-pixel diagonal displacement, 1.6 mm/pixel, visibility in only two consecutive frames, and 120 fps. The paper notes the limit can be lower when a particle is visible in more frames, because intermediate frames can be skipped.

relevant_methods.method: Per-particle crop background removal and segmentation (sizing stage only)
relevant_methods.details: Using 2D coordinates from the 3D-PTV output, each image is cropped and the median image of the prior 10 images is subtracted 'to improve particle isolation and remove background objects'. The boundary is then found with Otsu unsupervised threshold selection. The Otsu method 'was visually confirmed to perform very well overall in the current configurations'. The paper notes a possible failure mode, not a counted result: instances where a portion of the particle blends with the background 'may negatively influence edge detection in individual images'.
relevant_methods.location: Sect. 2.3, step 1 and the following paragraph

relevant_methods.details: All available 3D reconstructions of a particle, typically about 10 models, are re-oriented with PCA along their main axis, and their projected outlines are pooled into cumulative outline plots. The paper says aggregating multiple observations of the same particle 'helps minimize the weight of those sporadic cases' (background blending, hidden features) in the final sizing results.
relevant_methods.location: Sect. 2.3, step 3 and the following paragraph; Fig. 4

relevant_methods.details: A rotating punk stick (about 3.6 mm thick) on a metallic arm about 397 mm long, mounted on the shaft of a gear box motor controlled by a DC power supply. Its glowing lit end is a model firebrand. Measured radius, height and velocity are compared with values predicted from the setup geometry. This tests geometric tracking accuracy, not detection precision against distractors.

110 quasi-spherical particles in 5 size classes (6, 8, 10, 12, 14 mm) released randomly in space and time from a 50.8 cm x 76.2 cm platform with 19 equally distributed 16 mm holes, about 1.65 m above the optical table, lit by four 3200-lumen LED lights. Sect. 3.2 does not state the sphere material. The Sect. 3 introduction says the validation tests used combusting model embers and non-combusting white particles, so the LED-lit spheres were presumably the non-combusting ones. Measured size histograms are compared with known diameters. Size classes were deliberately close together to make the test stringent.

relevant_methods.method: Validation design: real combusting firebrand shower with an independent reference
relevant_methods.details: A firebrand generator at the NIST National Fire Research Laboratory, fed 350 g of dry (moisture content < 6%) Douglas fir cuboids, produced firebrands for about 74 s. The Sect. 4.2 analysis covers a 35 s peak production window. Water pans covering about 2.4 m2 collected most of the landing firebrands (999 in all), which were dried and measured in 2D as an independent size reference. The comparison is distribution against distribution, not per-particle matching. The lighting conditions for this test are not described.

relevant_methods.method: Count metric from particle crossings and its sensitivity check
relevant_methods.details: Cumulative Particle Count (CPC, unit particles m-2) is defined from 'the number of particles crossing a reference surface of defined geometry and location', expressed per unit area of that surface. The reference surface is a disk (center X = -150 mm, Y = 1000 mm, Z = 0 mm; radius 200 mm) placed in the core of the flow at mid-height of the control volume. Particle Number Flux (PNF, particles m-2 s-1) is derived from the time-resolved CPC, with derivations over a 30 timestep window, stated as about 1 s in the Fig. 8 caption. Sensitivity was tested by changing the disk area by plus or minus 15%. A 'firebrand rose' repeats CPC and PNF over reference-surface orientations in 15 degree increments, keeping the surface center fixed.

A fictitious 25.4 mm sphere is moved through the control volume and its visual hull reconstructed for two positions of Camera 4. Normalized volume (reconstructed over known volume) is plotted against the mean camera-to-particle distance. As future work, the paper proposes a hybrid approach with a deep learning shape classifier, supported by synthetic data generation, to correct sizing bias.

reported_results_with_definitions: Fragmentation statistic (Sect. 4.1). 'On a total number of 640 expected (complete) trajectories, 6.4% were found incomplete and were successfully recombined, and 0.8% could not be recombined.' Population: airborne firebrands from the NIST NFRL generator test (Douglas fir cuboids), 4-camera 3D-PTV. The sentence is in Sect. 4.1 and does not itself name a time window, though the Sect. 4.2 analysis uses the 35 s peak window. The main text does not say how the 640 'expected' trajectories were established, how a recombination was verified as successful, or what temporal window was used. This is a fragmentation rate, not a precision or spurious-track rate.

Raw trajectory count (Sect. 4.2.1, Fig. 7). 691 raw 3D trajectories reconstructed 'in the present case' (the 35 s analysis window). The Conclusion describes this as nearly 700 firebrands successfully reconstructed over 35 s. The text does not reconcile 691 raw trajectories with 640 expected complete trajectories, and does not say whether 691 is before or after recombination.
No precision, false-positive, spurious-detection or spurious-track statistic is reported anywhere in the main text.

Calibration (Sect. 2.2). Expanded uncertainty in position of plus or minus 1.5 mm in all directions, corresponding to plus or minus 0.89 to 2.69 pixels across the control volume. Uncertainties in the paper are expanded with k = 2 (95%, assuming normality) unless stated otherwise.

Rotating punk stick tracking validation (Sect. 3.1). Measured radius 396.2 mm plus or minus 2.3 mm versus predicted 396.9 mm plus or minus 5 mm. Measured height 1526.9 mm plus or minus 3.7 mm versus predicted 1523.3 mm plus or minus 5 mm. Mean measured velocity 44.3 cm/s plus or minus 1.9 cm/s versus predicted 44.3 cm/s. Population: one glowing stick end on a known circular path.

Sphere sizing validation (Sect. 3.2). 110 particles by class, as count and true diameter: 6 mm (38, 6.2 plus or minus 0.2 mm), 8 mm (36, 7.9 plus or minus 0.3 mm), 10 mm (13, 9.9 plus or minus 0.2 mm), 12 mm (10, 11.9 plus or minus 0.2 mm), 14 mm (13, 13.8 plus or minus 0.4 mm). Results are qualitative only. The z* and x* measurements 'agreed relatively well' with known diameters. Shifts toward smaller classes are explained by an edge detection bias toward inner silhouette boundaries (-1 pixel against visual observation) caused by nonuniform illumination. Some y* measurements fall in classes 'well beyond the maximum sphere diameter' because of a nonsystematic Visual Hull artifact; Fig. 5b shows a 'worst case scenario' 14 mm sphere contributing to the 20 mm class (the histogram image itself was not seen). No numeric accuracy or error rate is given. The histogram class width is 2 mm.

Resolvability claims (Sect. 2.1). Expected detection of glowing particles from 2 mm to multi-centimeter lengths. Disks 51 mm wide were tracked and reconstructed in validation tests the paper does not report. Resolved velocities are expected from 0.27 m/s to at least 18 m/s for flow conditions similar to Sect. 4 and a data acquisition frequency of 120 fps. The lower limit assumes a 1-pixel image, a 1-pixel diagonal displacement, 1.6 mm/pixel and two-frame visibility.
Observed dynamics (Sect. 4.2.1). Low-velocity motion (< 0.4 m/s) of small embers and projectile-like motion (> 4 m/s) of gravity-driven embers were both captured in the NFRL test.

Count metric (Sect. 4.2.1, Fig. 8). Total CPC (particles crossing per m2 of reference surface) over the test was close to 1281 particles per m2 for the 200 mm radius reference disk. Increasing the disk area by 15% decreased CPC by 3.9%; decreasing it by 15% increased CPC by 5.2%. PNF peaked at 111 particles per m2 per s at t = 9 s, with most values between 25 and 65 particles per m2 per s.

Firebrand rose (Sect. 4.2.1, Fig. 9). The highest total CPC in any orientation was 1329 particles per m2, recorded for orientations spanning theta = 15 degrees, phi = 225 to 285 degrees. In those orientations PNF exceeded 40 particles per m2 per s for more than one third of the test. For theta = 90 degrees, phi = 270 degrees (a vertical surface parallel to the generator exit plane), total CPC was about 573 particles per m2, with virtually no time above 40 particles per m2 per s.

Artificial versus field exposure (Sect. 4.2.2). Extrapolated time-averaged PNF for a ground-facing orientation (theta = 0, phi = 0) at a 120 mm collection height was 24.5 particles per m2 per s, or 21.5 accounting for the Z-axis ground offset. The authors estimate the highest firebrand flux in Thomas et al. 2017 (one prescribed fire, about 7 to 13 MW/m, pine-dominated ecosystem) as at most 7 particles per m2 per s, using peak collection durations of 67 to 122 s and total collected counts. The generator flux was therefore more than 3 times the maximum the authors estimated for that one prescribed fire study. This is not a general field maximum.

Sizing against ground collection (Sect. 4.2.3, Fig. 10). Qualitative only: distributions 'agree very well' for the longest dimension (y*) and one of the smaller dimensions (airborne x*) at 1 mm class width. Along z*, the paper says the distributions 'suggest' that 'some of the emberometer measurements overestimate the actual firebrand size'. Population: combusting cuboids (this test) and combusting sticks (Bouvet et al. 2018), each compared with 2D measurements of water-quenched collected firebrands. Average flight time from the control volume center to the ground was on the order of 0.3 s.

Reconstruction settings (Sect. 2.3). Monte Carlo sampling at 40 points per mm3, chosen to balance compute time against volume accuracy (> 95% of the true hull volume). The resolution calibration uncertainty is at most 0.1 mm/pixel at the farthest locations (about 2.4 m from the camera image planes).

Camera layout synthetic test (Sect. 5, Fig. 11). With Camera 4 moved out of plane, most data points for a 25.4 mm fictitious sphere fall below a 15% volume overestimation level, a marked improvement over the original layout.
must_not_transfer: The 6.4% recombined and 0.8% unrecoverable fragmentation rates. They come from a calibrated 4-camera 3D-PTV system (acquisition quoted at 120 fps in Sect. 2.1; effective tracking rate for this test not stated), a laboratory firebrand generator at NIST NFRL, Douglas fir cuboids and very low image density (about 4 x 10^-5 ppp). wfglink is single-camera RGB without depth, often compressed video, with uncontrolled backgrounds. These rates must not be quoted as expected or achievable wfglink fragmentation rates.

Do not treat the fragmentation statistic as precision or as a spurious-track rate. The paper reports no precision, false-positive or spurious-trajectory figure, so it cannot be cited as evidence for any precision level of an ember track verifier.

Reviewer inference, not a claim in the paper: the 4-view epipolar correspondence and triangulation probably keep many single-view artifacts from becoming 3D trajectories. The paper never discusses clutter, distractors or their rejection, so it must not be cited as showing that its trajectory set was clean. wfglink has no second view, so it would have no such filtering. Even if the multi-view trajectory set was clean, that would not imply a clean single-camera candidate set.

The claim that broken trajectories are 'seldom' holds, if at all, under the paper's conditions (low density, four views, tracking in image and object space). It must not be assumed for wfglink, where motion blur, compression, exposure changes and bright backgrounds are likely to fragment tracks more often.

Metric quantities (2 mm minimum size, 0.27 to 18 m/s velocity range, 1.6 mm/pixel, CPC and PNF in particles per m2 and per m2 per s, the firebrand rose) all need calibrated 3D positions and metric scale. wfglink counts are image-plane track counts, not fluxes per area, and must not be expressed in these units or compared with these values.

The recombination algorithm's parameters (temporal window, prediction model, matching thresholds) are not in this paper; they are deferred to NIST TN 2093, which was not read here. Do not attribute specific parameter values to this source.

'Confirmed to efficiently process glowing/hot particles' (intensity-weighted centroid) and Otsu thresholding 'visually confirmed to perform very well' are unquantified qualitative statements made under the paper's configurations. They are not evidence of detector performance on wildfire video.

The median of prior 10 frames background subtraction was applied only to crops around particles already located by 3D-PTV, for sizing, with fixed-position cameras. It was not a detection or verification step, and it was not validated against distractors.

The validation experiments test geometric tracking and sizing accuracy on known targets: one glowing stick end, and LED-lit quasi-spherical particles of known size (presumably the non-combusting white particles mentioned in Sect. 3). None measures rejection of non-ember lookalikes. They must not be presented as precision validation.
All Visual Hull sizing results, size histograms and the 15% volume overestimation figure depend on multi-view reconstruction. They have no meaning for single-camera wfglink.

The comparison with Thomas et al. 2017 (artificial flux more than 3 times the authors' estimated maximum for that one prescribed fire) is about how realistic the generator's exposure is. It says nothing about detection and must not be used to argue about ember density in wfglink clips.

The internal ambiguity between 691 raw trajectories, 640 expected complete trajectories and 'nearly 700 firebrands' is not resolved in the text. Do not derive a fragment-per-particle ratio or an overcount rate from these numbers.
proposed_adaptations: PROPOSED ADAPTATION: add image-plane gap bridging to the wfglink tracker, modeled on the paper's recombination idea. When a track ends early, predict its missing positions forward for a short user-set window of frames. Then link it to a 'sister' track that starts near the predicted position at a consistent time. The merged track counts once. In the causal verifier, the window must close before the accept or reject decision, so the bridging window bounds verifier latency. Window, motion model and thresholds must be chosen and validated on wfglink data, since the paper gives none.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: report fragmentation separately from precision, using the paper's three-way breakdown. On human-labeled wfglink clips, count expected complete ember tracks, the fraction that fragmented but were correctly re-linked, and the fraction that stayed fragmented. Also report spurious accepted tracks, a quantity the paper does not provide. This keeps fragmentation overcounting from being confused with false positives.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: build a known-trajectory true-positive check like the rotating punk stick. Film a glowing stick end on a motor-driven arm with known radius and angular speed using the single wfglink camera. Check that the tracker yields one continuous track per revolution segment, that the verifier accepts it, and that the fitted image-plane circle matches the geometry. This tests continuity and acceptance, not rejection of lookalikes. Any such rig must be run with appropriate fire safety supervision.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: add the condition the paper gives as an example cause of broken trajectories, a low-glow ember against a very bright background object, to the wfglink test sets for both the tracker and the verifier, as a hard true-positive case.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: in the small patch classifier input, add a causal background-subtracted channel. Subtract the median of the prior N frames from the crop around the candidate. The paper used N = 10, but only for sizing crops taken with fixed cameras. Validate on wfglink clips, because a moving camera, flicker or compression could make this channel misleading.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: decide per track rather than per frame. Pool patch classifier scores over the available observations of a track within the causal window. This borrows the paper's sizing rationale that aggregating multiple observations reduces the weight of sporadic bad frames. Set a minimum observation count before acceptance. The paper applied this to sizing, not to classification, so the benefit must be shown on wfglink data.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: derive per-clip resolvability limits the way the paper does (1-pixel minimum image size, 1-pixel minimum displacement, two-frame visibility), but in pixel and frame units. Use them to set minimum track length and minimum displacement rules. The paper resolved slow embers (< 0.4 m/s), so a strict minimum-motion rule may reject real slow embers. Check any such rule against labeled slow embers before adopting it.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: run a sensitivity check on counting-region parameters, as the paper varied disk area by plus or minus 15%. Report how wfglink accepted-track counts change when the counting region or line and the verifier thresholds are perturbed.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: when possible, compare wfglink counts with an independent reference of a different kind, such as an independent human count of the same clip window, as the paper compared airborne measurements with ground collection. Compare like populations and the same time window.
short_quotes: Although seldom, a broken trajectory can occur if a firebrand visibility becomes challenging (e.g., low glow versus very bright object in the background).

predict, within a user-specified temporal window, the missing positions of firebrands with early-ended trajectories and identify sister trajectories by performing spatio-temporal matching in each particle image plane
To support the airborne firebrand sizing analysis (and avoid counting broken tracks as independent particles), the trajectory recombination strategy described in Sect. 2.2 was applied.
On a total number of 640 expected (complete) trajectories, 6.4% were found incomplete and were successfully recombined, and 0.8% could not be recombined.

The firebrand exposure can be quantified by monitoring the number of particles crossing a reference surface of defined geometry and location within the experimental control volume, therefore yielding a Cumulative Particle Count (CPC, unit: particles m−2).

problems.claim: Count metric (relevant_methods): 'Cumulative Particle Count (CPC) is the number of trajectories crossing a reference disk'.
problems.issue: Definition is not exact. Sect. 4.2.1 defines CPC from 'the number of particles crossing a reference surface of defined geometry and location', with unit particles m-2, so it is normalized by the surface area. It counts particles, not trajectories, which matters here because broken tracks are the topic. The area normalization is also why a larger disk gives a lower CPC.
problems.correction: CPC (unit particles m-2) is defined from 'the number of particles crossing a reference surface of defined geometry and location', expressed per unit area of that surface. The surface is a disk (center X = -150 mm, Y = 1000 mm, Z = 0 mm; radius 200 mm). Add the verbatim CPC definition sentence to short_quotes.

problems.claim: must_not_transfer item 1: the fragmentation rates 'come from a calibrated 4-camera 3D-PTV system at 120 fps'.
problems.issue: The text gives 120 fps only in Sect. 2.1, as the acquisition frequency assumed for the expected velocity limits. It never states the tracking frame rate for the NFRL test. The Fig. 8 caption equates a 30 timestep window with about 1 s, which implies about 30 timesteps per second, and Sect. 2.1 says sequences can be downsampled for tracking. The record states 120 fps as a fact about the test, and the text does not support that.
problems.correction: Say acquisition is quoted at 120 fps in Sect. 2.1 but the effective tracking rate for the NFRL test is not stated. Note in the acquisition method that Fig. 8 equates a 30 timestep window with about 1 s, which the text does not reconcile with 120 fps.

problems.claim: must_not_transfer item 4: 'seldom' breaks hold 'under the paper's conditions (low density, controlled lighting, multiple views, tracking in object space)'.
problems.issue: Lighting for the NFRL firebrand test is not described. The LED lighting in the text belongs only to the sphere validation (Sect. 3.2). The paper's own example of a break cause is a very bright background object, so 'controlled lighting' is not supported. Tracking also uses both image-space and object-space information, not object space alone.
problems.correction: Replace with '(low density, four views, tracking in image and object space)' and drop 'controlled lighting'. Add to the NFRL method that the lighting conditions for that test are not described.

problems.claim: Method title 'Multi-view correspondence and 3D triangulation (implicit consistency filter)' and must_not_transfer item 3: 'The paper's low clutter partly comes from the epipolar and triangulation consistency across four views ... distractors that this system rejects implicitly'.
problems.issue: The paper says nothing about clutter, distractors, or epipolar matching rejecting spurious detections. Presenting this as a property of the paper over-claims. It is the reviewer's inference.
problems.correction: Remove '(implicit consistency filter)' from the method name. Reword item 3 as 'Reviewer inference, not a claim in the paper', and say that the paper never discusses clutter, distractors or their rejection, so it cannot be cited as showing its trajectory set was clean.

problems.claim: Recombination method: 'The stated purpose in Sect. 4.1 is to avoid counting broken tracks as independent particles.'
problems.issue: Incomplete. The sentence gives the main purpose as 'To support the airborne firebrand sizing analysis', and avoiding double counting appears only in parentheses as a second aim.
problems.correction: The stated purpose is 'to support the airborne firebrand sizing analysis', with avoiding counting broken tracks as independent particles given in parentheses as a second aim.

problems.claim: Recombination method: 'Breaks are described as seldom and attributed to cases where a firebrand's visibility becomes challenging'.
problems.issue: Slightly overstated. The paper says a break 'can occur if' visibility becomes challenging and gives one example. It does not attribute all breaks to this cause.
problems.correction: Say that, 'although seldom', a break 'can occur if' visibility becomes challenging, with one example (low glow against a very bright background object), and that the paper gives no full list of causes. Proposed adaptation 4 should likewise refer to the single example condition (a hard true-positive case), not to 'distractor cases the paper names as fragmentation causes'.

problems.claim: Otsu segmentation: 'The paper notes failures where part of the particle blends with the background.'
problems.issue: Overstated. The paper says such instances 'may negatively influence edge detection in individual images', which is a possible failure mode. It reports no observed or counted failures.
problems.correction: The paper notes, as a possible failure mode rather than a counted result, that instances where a portion of the particle blends with the background 'may negatively influence edge detection in individual images'.
