relevant_methods.details: The CNN classifies each view of an already detected and 3D-tracked airborne firebrand as 'flaming' or 'smoldering'. Every input is a known firebrand. The paper has no background, clutter or non-firebrand class and no detection step inside the CNN. Each quadrant 'may be independently rated' flaming or smoldering, and a firebrand can be flaming in some views and smoldering in others at the same time step (the 'Mixed' column of Fig. 2). So the unit that is labeled and classified is a single image (one view at one time step). The paper does not state whether a particle's label can change from one time step to the next, and it also describes the 293 particles as 'hand labeled as smoldering or flaming'.

relevant_methods.method: Upstream detection and tracking (not part of the CNN)
relevant_methods.details: The Emberometer combines 3D Particle Tracking Velocimetry and 3D Particle Shape Reconstruction with four cameras. Video frames are extracted as high bit depth color sequences with commercial software. An in-house MATLAB code synchronizes them and converts them to low bit depth grayscale. The grayscale sequences are 'processed by the PTV software' (the paper does not say whether it is commercial or in-house), and in-house FORTRAN routines assemble each particle's full 3D motion history and patch broken trajectories. The classifier uses high bit depth color crops (background subtracted), cropped and numbered from the final tracking outputs. A quadrant is entirely black when the firebrand was not detected in that view at that time step (not visible, or detected but the particle correspondence step failed). Black quadrants are identified automatically and removed from CNN analysis.
relevant_methods.location: Section 2, pp.3 to 4; Section 3, p.4; Figure 2 caption, p.5

relevant_methods.details: Each camera view of a firebrand at one time step goes to the CNN on its own as an RGB image of 71 x 71 pixels, for both training and routine classification. Up to four views make up a 'quadview', but the views are not fused. CNN inputs are background subtracted (Section 2 text and Fig. 2 caption). The paper does not say how the 71 x 71 crop is placed or scaled relative to particle size, what the background model is, or whether the high bit depth was kept at the CNN input. It also does not say how the 71 x 71 crops were resized to the input sizes the pretrained networks expect.
relevant_methods.location: Section 3, p.4; Section 2, p.4; Figure 2, p.5

relevant_methods.details: Four Sony DSC-RX10M3 compact cameras (about 20 megapixels) with large diameter built-in lenses. The cameras were given full spectrum conversion and fitted with Hoya R72 infrared filters 'ensuring light transmission above 760 nm', 'to enhance firebrand detection'. They sit in hard shells with quartz windows on a collapsible X-shaped aluminum stand. Video is recorded and frames are extracted with commercial software. The paper states no frame rate, exposure or resolution of the extracted frames. The example frame in Fig. 1b looks magenta-toned (checker and extractor visual observation, not a statement in the text).

Outdoor deployment at the Frederick County Public Safety Training Facility, Frederick, MD, downstream of a firebrand generator (a centrifugal blower in line with cylindrical stainless-steel duct elements). Fuel was 350 g plus or minus 1 g of dry (moisture under 6 %) birch/maple dowels, 6.4 mm diameter and 51 mm long, with chamfered edges. The background was asphalt, forested areas with mixed vegetation, and clear sky. The text does not state the time of day.

293 particles were 'carefully reviewed and hand labeled as smoldering or flaming'. The review covered all time steps and quadrant views available for each firebrand, excluding black quadrants and quadrants where large flames attributed to the firebrand generator were visible. Labeling used color images without background subtraction, 'allowing for detailed dynamic examination of the firebrand silhouettes across time steps'. So labelers had temporal context that the single-frame CNN does not have (extractor inference). This produced 23,873 labeled images. The paper does not say how many people labeled and reports no inter-labeler agreement.

88.8 % of the labeled images were smoldering. To avoid bias, the authors drew a random subset of smoldering images equal in size to the flaming set (about 2,700 each). The balanced set was split randomly into training (80 %), validation (10 %) and test (10 %) and held constant across all CNNs. The paper describes no grouping by particle, time step or view, so images of the same firebrand (other time steps or other views) can appear in more than one split (extractor inference from 'separated randomly'). About 18,500 leftover smoldering images, 'previously set apart during the training dataset generation step', were later classified with the chosen model.

Seven layers in Fig. 3: L1 conv + batch norm + ReLU, L2 max pool 2x2 stride 2, L3 conv + BN + ReLU, L4 max pool 2x2 stride 2, L5 conv + BN + ReLU, L6 fully connected (2 outputs), L7 softmax. Feature maps run 71x71, then 35x35, then 17x17. The filter configurations (Table 1) are A: 3x3 with 28, 22, 16 filters; B: 3x3 with 64, 128, 256; C: 5x5 with 28, 22, 16; D: 7x7 with 28, 22, 16. Parametric tests varied filter size and filter count. Adding convolutional layers had little effect. Table 1 shows only 'A representative subset' of the configurations; other filter combinations were trained but 'the performance metrics were lower than those presented'. The paper does not say whether the shown configurations were picked on validation or test results.
relevant_methods.location: Section 3, p.4; Section 4, p.7; Figure 3, p.6; Table 1, p.7

relevant_methods.method: Transfer learning on five ImageNet-pretrained networks (E to I)
relevant_methods.details: The PDF describes them by structure only. E: 5 conv and 3 FC layers, 61 million parameters, overlapping pooling and local response normalization. F: 22 layers, 7 million parameters, 9 inception modules. G: bottleneck design, 18 layers, 11.7 million parameters, residual mapping, skip connections, heavy batch norm. H: 18 layers, 1.24 million parameters, 8 fire modules. I: 16 layers, 138 million parameters, all 3x3 convolutions. They were 'chosen due to availability, prevalence in the literature, and variation in architecture'. The NIST landing page abstract names the set as AlexNet, GoogLeNet, ResNet-18, SqueezeNet and VGG-16 and says the chosen one is GoogLeNet; since the PDF says the chosen one is CNN F, F is GoogLeNet. Matching E, G, H and I one by one to the other names is extractor inference from the structure descriptions; the PDF does not state it.
relevant_methods.location: Section 3, pp.4 to 5; NIST landing page abstract

relevant_methods.details: MATLAB Deep Learning Toolbox (MATLAB 2022, reference [19] gives R2022a). Learning rate 0.0001, chosen from validation loss trends. The number of iterations was set by a validation patience of 5. For the transfer learning cases only, 'the learning rate for the weights and biases was increased by a factor of ten' to shorten training (the paper does not say which layers this applied to), and the mini-batch size was varied between 5 and 15: 5 gave the Table 1 results and 10 and 15 were 'marginally worse for every pretrained CNN'. The mini-batch size for lightweight CNNs A to D is not stated. No optimizer is named. Hardware: Intel i7-8700 with NVIDIA Quadro P1000 (4 GB). CNN I used a Xeon W-1370P with Quadro RTX 4000 (8 GB). The paper reports no data augmentation and no inference speed.

Accuracy (Eq. 1) and per-class precision, recall and F-measure (Eqs. 2 and 3). Validation and test accuracy were compared to check for overfitting, and per-class F-measures to check bias. The final choice weighed the performance metrics and 'memory requirements': those of E and I were about 10 and 22 times that of F, and I needed additional computing resources. These ratios match the Table 1 size-on-disk column (202/21.2 is about 9.5 and 477/21.2 is about 22.5, checker arithmetic). The conclusions describe the basis as 'accuracy, F-measure, and size metrics'. CNN F was chosen. The paper gives no confidence intervals and no repeated runs or seeds.
relevant_methods.location: Section 3.1, pp.6 to 7; Section 4, pp.7 to 8; Section 5, p.8

reported_results_with_definitions: Dataset size: 293 hand-labeled particles gave 23,873 single-view, single-time-step images labeled flaming or smoldering, after excluding black quadrants and quadrants showing large generator flames. 88.8 % were smoldering. Source: one outdoor Emberometer test with birch/maple dowels from a blower-driven firebrand generator. The Introduction says the whole dataset holds 'over 71,000 individual firebrand images'; only the 23,873 hand-labeled images have any reported accuracy.

Balanced training pool: about 2,700 flaming images plus about 2,700 randomly selected smoldering images, split randomly into 80 % training, 10 % validation and 10 % test (the paper says the images were 'separated randomly'; no grouping is described). Extractor arithmetic from the stated numbers, not stated in the paper: the validation and test sets each hold about 540 images.

Accuracy is defined as true predictions divided by total predictions (Eq. 1). Precision = TP/(TP+FP) and Recall = TP/(TP+FN), computed per class with the hand label as ground truth (Eq. 2). F is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, F = 2 x Precision x Recall / (Precision + Recall), per class (Eq. 3).

Table 1, lightweight CNNs (validation accuracy %, test accuracy %, F flaming, F smoldering, size on disk MB): A (3x3, 28/22/16) 88.9, 89.1, 0.89, 0.89, 0.07. B (3x3, 64/128/256) 91.8, 92.0, 0.92, 0.92, 1.84. C (5x5, 28/22/16) 90.2, 90.4, 0.90, 0.91, 0.16. D (7x7, 28/22/16) 91.2, 90.8, 0.90, 0.91, 0.23. Population: the accuracy columns are on the balanced validation and test splits respectively. Table 1 does not say which split (validation, test or both) the F-measure columns were computed on.

Table 1, transfer learning with mini-batch 5 (validation accuracy %, test accuracy %, F flaming, F smoldering, size on disk MB): E 94.76, 95.30, 0.95, 0.95, 202. F 95.1, 95.1, 0.95, 0.95, 21.2. G 95.3, 93.8, 0.94, 0.94, 39.7. H 93.8, 92.5, 0.92, 0.93, 2.59. I 95.9, 95.7, 0.96, 0.96, 477. Same populations as above: accuracy on the balanced validation and test splits; the split behind the F-measures is not stated.

For lightweight configuration B the text gives flaming precision 0.93, flaming recall 0.91, smoldering precision 0.91 and smoldering recall 0.93. It does not say whether these are validation or test figures. The text says the best accuracy 'for the validation and test sets was just under 92 %' while Table 1 lists 91.8 for validation and 92.0 for test.

CNN G's test accuracy was '1.5 % lower than the validation set' (95.3 vs 93.8 in Table 1, so 1.5 percentage points), which the authors read as 'possibly indicating some overfitting'. Mini-batch sizes 10 and 15 were 'marginally worse' for every pretrained CNN, with no numbers given.
Memory: the 'memory requirements' of E and I were about 10 and 22 times that of F. Checker arithmetic: this matches the size-on-disk ratios in Table 1 (202/21.2 and 477/21.2).

The chosen model (transfer learning on CNN F, GoogLeNet per the landing page) was run on about 18,500 leftover smoldering images 'previously set apart during the training dataset generation step', with 95.4 % accuracy. These are the hand-labeled smoldering images not drawn into the balanced subset, so they come from the same 293 particles (23,873 x 0.888 is about 21,200 smoldering images; minus about 2,700 sampled leaves about 18,500, checker arithmetic). The paper does not say whether the smoldering subsample was drawn by image or by particle, so other images of the same particles (other time steps and views) were very likely in the training set. Every image in this population is hand-labeled smoldering, so this figure is effectively the smoldering-class recall on those images, not two-class accuracy (extractor interpretation from the definitions).

Headline figures: the abstract reports about 92 % accuracy for the best lightweight CNN and 'around 95 %' for the pretrained CNNs, evaluated 'on an unseen subset of the data'. The conclusions say CNN F gave 'predictions systematically exceeding 95 % accuracy for the validation and test sets considered' (Table 1: 95.1 and 95.1). All of these are flaming-vs-smoldering accuracy on image crops of already-tracked firebrands from a balanced, randomly split, single-experiment dataset.
must_not_transfer: The ~95 % figure must not be cited as ember detection accuracy, precision or recall for wfglink. It measures flaming vs smoldering among crops already known to be firebrands, found by a four-camera 3D tracker. The paper has no background, clutter or non-ember class, so it says nothing about how well a CNN rejects false candidates such as lights, reflections, sun glints, insects or compression artifacts. This paper is not an ember-versus-background detector.

The trained weights and the reported results are not a validated RGB ember detector and must not be treated as one. The paper does not say the weights were released. Even if they were, they are MATLAB models trained on imagery from full-spectrum cameras behind 760 nm infrared filters, for a different two-class task.

The image colors are not ordinary visible-light RGB. The paper states the cameras 'have undergone full spectrum conversion and are equipped with infrared filters (Hoya R72) ensuring light transmission above 760 nm'. Extractor inference, not stated in the paper: the R72 is a longpass filter, so the RGB channels of these cameras mainly record near-infrared light, consistent with the magenta-toned frame in Fig. 1b. wfglink uses ordinary visible-light RGB video, so color statistics, hue thresholds and learned features do not carry over.

Detection quality depends on the multi-camera stereo rig. Particles must be found and matched across up to four synchronized views, and failed correspondence produces black quadrants that are dropped. wfglink has one camera with no depth and no cross-view consistency check, so the candidate population reaching a wfglink verifier will be much noisier than the population this CNN saw.

The 95 % numbers come from a random split of images from only 293 particles, with many time steps and up to four views per particle (about 81 images per particle on average, extractor arithmetic). Nothing indicates grouping by particle, so near-duplicate frames of the same firebrand probably appear in training and test. Treat the numbers as optimistic even for unseen particles in the same test, and as untested for new scenes, fuels, cameras or days.

All data come from one outdoor experiment with one fuel (birch/maple dowels), one artificial generator and one background setting. The paper reports no cross-scene, cross-day or real-wildfire generalization.

Evaluation used a 50/50 class-balanced set, but the natural ratio was 88.8 % smoldering. Balanced-set accuracy or F-measure does not give precision at natural prevalence. wfglink's ember vs non-ember prevalence is different again, so no precision expectation should be carried over.

The 95.4 % on about 18,500 leftover smoldering images is a single-class (smoldering recall) figure on the remainder of the same hand-labeled pool from the 293 particles whose other images were used for training. It is not an independent test and not a second two-class accuracy.

Pairwise accuracy differences among E, F, G and I in Table 1 are about 0.2 to 1.9 percentage points (test: 93.8 to 95.7; validation: 94.76 to 95.9), from one fixed split of about 540 test images, with no repeats or confidence intervals. Extractor estimate, not from the paper: one binomial standard error near 95 % with n of about 540 is about 0.9 percentage points. So the paper does not show that GoogLeNet-style transfer learning beats the other choices in general, and it gives no basis for picking a backbone for wfglink.
The paper reports no inference speed or latency. The size-on-disk column and the training GPUs (Quadro P1000, RTX 4000) say nothing about real-time throughput on wfglink hardware.

The CNN inputs were background subtracted, but the paper does not describe the background model or the crop scaling. Its 71 x 71 setting and the missing resize step for the pretrained nets cannot be copied as a validated recipe.

Human labelers examined color images without background subtraction across time steps, while the CNN classifies single background-subtracted frames. The reported agreement is with those temporally informed labels, not with any physical ground truth such as temperature. The number of labelers and any inter-labeler agreement are not reported.
proposed_adaptations: PROPOSED ADAPTATION: Copy only the pipeline shape. The patch classifier sees fixed-size crops from tracker output, as here, but wfglink's verifier needs a third kind of example the paper never had: explicit negatives (non-ember blobs such as lights, glints, foliage highlights, compression flicker, insects) from wfglink's own clips. The target becomes ember vs non-ember, not flaming vs smoldering.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: Start with a tiny from-scratch CNN like their Figure 3 design (three conv+BN+ReLU blocks with two 2x2 max pools, an FC layer to 2 outputs, softmax, crops around 64 to 72 px). It is 0.07 to 1.84 MB on disk. On their two-class task the best such net (B) was about 3 points below the chosen CNN F (92.0 vs 95.1 test, 91.8 vs 95.1 validation) and the smallest (A) about 6 points below (89.1 vs 95.1 test). Move to a small pretrained backbone only if grouped held-out evaluation on wfglink data shows a clear gain.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: Split train, validation and test by clip and by track, never by individual frame, so frames of one ember or one false blob never appear in two splits. Report precision with confidence intervals at the natural candidate prevalence of held-out clips, not on a balanced set.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: Their labels could differ between views of the same firebrand at one time step (the 'Mixed' firebrands), so a single crop can be ambiguous. Score each frame's patch and combine the scores causally along the track (for example, average the log odds over the first N frames, with a minimum track length) before accepting a track into counts. Calibrate the acceptance threshold for high precision on validation data at natural prevalence.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: Mirror their imbalance handling but keep the evaluation honest. Subsample the majority class for training, then set thresholds on an unbalanced validation set. Like their leftover-smoldering check, keep a large negatives-only pool (clips with no embers) to estimate the false acceptance rate per track or per minute directly, but draw it from clips not used for training, which their leftover pool was not.
PROPOSED ADAPTATION: Treat frames where the tracker has no measurement (their black-quadrant case) as missing, and skip them instead of feeding empty crops to the classifier.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: Label at the track level while viewing temporal context and raw frames (as their annotators did), then carry labels to frames and record exceptions per frame. Their 23,873 crops came from 293 particles seen by up to four cameras (about 81 crops per particle), so a single-camera track yields roughly a quarter as many crops per track, and the paper never tested particle-grouped generalization. Treat their effort only as a rough scale, not as evidence that a few hundred tracks suffice.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: Test whether a background-difference channel added to the raw RGB crop helps, since their inputs were background subtracted. Decide only from grouped held-out results, because a moving or shaking single camera makes background subtraction less reliable than on their fixed rig.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: Use their training conventions only as starting points: a fixed held-constant split for comparing models, early stopping with a validation patience around 5, learning rate around 1e-4, small mini-batches. Select the model on precision, size and measured latency on wfglink hardware together, as they weighed accuracy against footprint when choosing F over I.

So they are the rest of the same 23,873 hand-labeled images from the 293 particles. The counts agree: 23,873 x 0.888 is about 21,200 smoldering images, and minus about 2,700 sampled that leaves about 18,500. problems.claim: Table 1 rows, 'Population: the balanced validation and test splits described above' (reported_results #4 and #5).

problems.claim: Method 1: 'labels are per view and per time step, not per particle'. Proposed adaptation #4: 'Their labels varied by view and by time step (the mixed firebrands)'.
problems.issue: The paper says each quadrant 'may be independently rated'. The 'Mixed' column of Fig. 2 shows labels differing between views at a single time step. proposed_adaptations: PROPOSED ADAPTATION: Use a small U-Net style network as an optional mask refiner on fixed-size crops around tracker candidates (for example 32x32 or 64x64), not on full frames. Pass mask-derived features (mask area, compactness, peak and mean intensity inside the mask, mask stability across frames) to the patch classifier and the temporal classifier, instead of using the mask itself as the accept decision.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: Because the abstract reports only an undefined accuracy, wfglink should fix its own metric definitions before training. Track-level precision = accepted tracks that match a labelled ember track divided by all accepted tracks. Track-level recall = labelled ember tracks matched by an accepted track divided by all labelled ember tracks. Any pixel IoU or Dice for a mask refiner should be reported separately and never presented as a detection metric.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: The abstract's 'limited training data' remark is reason enough to test a low-label regime, but only as a hypothesis. Run a learning curve on wfglink's own labelled patches with hard negatives (flame edges, reflections, headlights, streetlights, sensor hot pixels) and report precision at a fixed operating point for each training-set size.

PROPOSED ADAPTATION: If controlled footage (wind tunnel or lab burns) is used, use it mainly as a source of positive ember patches. relevant_methods.method: Dataset structure: fixed-view camera sequences that include frames from before ignition
relevant_methods.details: 315 fire sequences from 101 HPWREN cameras across 30 stations (June 2016 to July 2021), on remote mountain tops in Southern California. Each sequence typically covers 40 min before to 40 min after the start of the fire at about 60 s spacing, for a total of 81 images per sequence. The paper says these images serve as binary smoke/no-smoke labels for each image. Section 6.3 adds that the ground truth labels were created by a human expert with full temporal context (all past and future frames) to precisely determine the first frame in which smoke is visible, so the positive onset is the expert-judged first visible-smoke frame. 24,800 images at 1536x2048 or 2048x3072. 114 fires are missing on average 6.6 images each. Section 7.2 says the dataset contains roughly 50% positive and 50% negative examples. The paper gives no camera-to-fire distance.

relevant_methods.method: Exclusion of out-of-distribution sequences before splitting
relevant_methods.details: Removed black and white image fires (N=10), night fires (N=19) and fires where smoke presence was questionable (N=16, including one fire with 180 images and no labels). In total 45 fires and 3,700 images were removed. The exact lists were published, and the published lists have 10, 19 and 16 names.

relevant_methods.method: Grouped split by fire sequence, not by image
relevant_methods.details: Train = the 144 fires whose smoke was manually annotated with bounding boxes and contour masks (53.3% of eligible fires, 11,300 images; Section 4.1 notes some positive images in them still lack masks). The remaining 126 fires (9,800 images) went to validation (64 fires, 4.9K images) and test (62 fires, 4.9K images), with roughly equal image counts. The authors justify the fire-level split as avoiding a model being evaluated on images of fires it already trained on through other frames of the video sequence. The training share is unusually small because the model needs annotations for training and only 144 annotated fires were available, and the authors did not want to omit fires from the evaluation sets. My own check of the published lists (not a claim in the paper): the split unit is one camera's sequence of one fire, not a physical fire event. Example: the named event 20200601_WILDLAND-DRILLS has 4 camera sequences in train and 1 (om-e-mobo-c) in test. 46 of the 62 test sequences come from a camera string that also has a train sequence (47 if the trailing -c or -m is ignored; 53 if validation cameras are included). 17 of the 20 test station prefixes also appear in train. 7 named date-plus-name events span more than one split: 5 span validation and test (20200806 SpringsFire, 20200822 SloaneFire, 20200828 BorderFire, 20200905 ValleyFire, 20201216 ChaparralFire), 1 spans train and test (20200601 WILDLAND-DRILLS) and 1 spans train and validation (20190803 OtaySouth). 21 more date-plus-generic-'FIRE' keys span splits (20 if the hyphenated train name 20190825_FIRE-smer-tcs8-mobo-c is not parsed), 3 of them (20190826, 20191003, 20191006) across all three splits; these may or may not be the same physical fire. Date-plus-name keys can also miss shared events named differently on the same date (for example 20190814 appears as Border in validation and FIRE in test).

relevant_methods.method: Preprocessing to suppress cloud false positives
relevant_methods.details: Resize to the empirically determined 1392x1856 to improve training and inference speed, then crop the top 352 rows, 'specifically determined to ensure that only rows well above the horizon are cropped to reduce false positives from clouds'. Final input is 1040x1856. Random augmentations: horizontal flip, vertical crop, color jitter, brightness and contrast jitter, blur. Normalization uses 0.5 mean and 0.5 standard deviation.

relevant_methods.method: Tiling with tile-level weak labels derived from masks
relevant_methods.details: 224x224 tiles overlapping by 20 px, 45 tiles per image (building on Govil et al. 2020). A tile is positive if the number of smoke pixels, from the filled contour-mask polygon, is greater than 250 (0.5% of the tile's pixels). The threshold was chosen in sequential tuning from {0, 10, 100, 250} pixels per tile. Where masks were missing but boxes existed, boxes were filled as polygons (486 images). 1,213 positive images (about 20%) lacked contour masks. The remaining 727 positive images without any usable annotation were not trained on, because using image-only feedback or copying masks from the closest available frame did not improve performance. Tile labels exist only for the training data.

relevant_methods.method: Spatiotemporal architecture (SmokeyNet): per-tile CNN, then per-tile LSTM over frames, then ViT across tiles
relevant_methods.details: Input is the tiled current frame plus its previous frame in the sequence (frames are about 60 s apart). An ImageNet-pretrained ResNet34 embeds each tile of the two frames independently. An LSTM combines each tile from the current frame with its counterpart in the previous frame. A ViT then incorporates information across all tiles. The ViT CLS token feeds an image head (FC layers of 256, 64, 1 with ReLU, sigmoid, threshold 0.5). Variants tested: other backbones (MobileNetV3Large, MobileNet plus FPN, EfficientNet-B0, DeiT-Tiny); 3 input frames; a transformer in place of the LSTM; a CNN plus ResNet18-3D in place of LSTM plus ViT; MOG2 background subtraction as an extra input channel through a separate CNN and LSTM, tested with the MobileNet backbone (Appendix C).
relevant_methods.location: Section 4.2; Section 5.1; Figure 2; Appendix C; Table 2

relevant_methods.method: Image-level decision from tile predictions for non-ViT baselines
relevant_methods.details: Without a CLS token, the image prediction comes from one fully connected layer with sigmoid over the tile predictions. The authors also tried the rule that if any tile prediction is positive the image is positive, and say it 'resulted in worse performance' (no numbers given). For detectors (Faster R-CNN, Mask R-CNN), an image is positive if any box scores above 0.5; thresholds {0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6} were tested.

relevant_methods.method: Loss design with intermediate tile supervision and positive weighting
relevant_methods.details: Image BCE with positive weight 5, chosen in sequential tuning from {1, 2, 5, 10}. The paper says the positive weight can be increased 'to trade off precision for higher recall', and that the value five was used 'to achieve more balanced precision and recall and improve the overall accuracy and F1-score'. Tile heads on the CNN, LSTM and ViT outputs each get a BCE term with positive weight 40, the ratio of negative to positive tiles. Total loss = image BCE + sum over tiles of the CNN, LSTM and ViT tile BCEs. The validation loss used for early stopping is the average number of image prediction errors, because tile labels exist only for the training data.
relevant_methods.location: Section 4.3; Appendix B equations 1 to 6; Section 5.2

relevant_methods.details: Hyperparameters were tuned sequentially, carrying the best result forward, in this order: learning rate, weight decay, image resize, tile smoke threshold, dropout, image positive weight. Final settings: SGD, learning rate 0.001, weight decay 0.001, no dropout, per-step batch 2 or 4 with gradient accumulation to an effective batch of 32, 25 epochs, trained on a single NVIDIA 2080Ti. The model with the lowest validation loss was used for evaluation on the test set. The text does not say which split or metric judged each tuning step.

relevant_methods.method: Evaluation metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, time-to-detection, size, speed
relevant_methods.details: Accuracy = (TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN). Precision = TP/(TP+FP). Recall = TP/(TP+FN). F1 = 2PR/(P+R). They are computed between model predictions and ground truth labels; Section 6.1 calls the headline figure image accuracy, and Table 2 is on the test set. Average time-to-detection (TTD) = 'the number of minutes until the model correctly predicts the first positive frame of a wildfire sequence, averaged over all fires'. The text does not state the time origin, how sequences that are never detected count toward TTD (one test fire, DeLuz, was 'completely missed'), or how TTD is combined across the five runs. My reading, not stated in the paper: false positives before the positive onset are not correct positive predictions, so they do not shorten TTD. Parameter count (M) and inference time (ms/image) are also reported; the hardware and measurement setup for inference time are not stated. Table 2 values average five runs, and no spread (standard deviation or interval) is reported for any model.

The introduction names transparent and amorphous smoke, faint, small or dissipating plumes, and false positives from clouds, fog and haze as the main difficulties. Figure 1 shows negatives with strong glare and misleading haze. Error analysis: systematic false positives from low-altitude clouds (three named test sequences). One fire was completely missed because its smoke was directly behind a transmission tower. The Figure 3 caption lists common misses (faint smoke at the start, dissipating smoke at the end) and common false positives (low-altitude clouds and haze). Figure 3 shows per-fire correct and incorrect predictions across negative and positive images (caption only read).

Three lab members experienced in classifying images for wildfire smoke. One image was randomly selected from each of the 62 test fires, and each was shown preceded by its previous frame, to replicate the model's temporal context and a real-time inference scenario. The authors note the ground truth was made by an expert with full past and future context, which makes early faint or small smoke hard to judge from one previous frame.

relevant_methods.method: Hard-negative mining without contaminating the holdout (proposed by the authors, not done)
relevant_methods.details: Future work proposes adding holdout false positives to training, as Govil et al. did. To keep the holdout's integrity, the authors say they would have to split the holdout set in two and leave one part untouched (relative sizes not stated). Other proposals: candidate smoke patch extraction before the model (ViBe background removal, YUV color segmentation, dark channel prior), fire location, date and weather data from historical records, unlabeled HPWREN Archive data with human-validated predictions, DINO self-supervision, GAN-synthesized smoke, pruning and distillation.

relevant_methods.method: Prevalence caveat and critique of a leaky prior evaluation
relevant_methods.details: The authors state that the roughly 50/50 balance is not representative of real-world scenarios and 'may induce models to incur a higher false positive rate on real-world data'. They criticize Govil et al. (2020) for a test set of 250 hand-selected images that contained images from the same video sequences as training, with only 10 min (10 frames) of separation, which may overstate performance.

reported_results_with_definitions: SmokeyNet (ResNet34 + LSTM + ViT, 2 frames): accuracy 83.49%, F1 82.59%, precision 89.84%, recall 76.45%, average TTD 3.12 min, 56.9M params, 51.6 ms/image. Image-level binary smoke classification at a sigmoid threshold of 0.5 on the FIgLib test split (62 fire sequences, about 4.9K images; the paper states the whole dataset is roughly 50/50 but does not report the test split's class balance), averaged over five runs with no spread reported. TTD is minutes until the model correctly predicts the first positive frame of a sequence, averaged over fires. The paper does not state the hardware used to measure inference time (Section 5.2 names a single NVIDIA 2080Ti only for training).

ResNet34 + LSTM + ViT with 3 frames: A 83.62, F1 82.83, P 90.85, R 76.11, TTD 2.94 min, 56.9M params, 80.3 ms/image. Same test population and definitions. The paper says one additional frame 'only marginally improves performance at the cost of a 55.6% increase in inference time'.

Ablations on the same test population and definitions (A / F1 / P / R / TTD min / params M / ms per image): ResNet34 alone, 1 frame: 79.40 / 78.90 / 81.62 / 76.58 / 2.81 / 22.3 / 29.7. ResNet34 + LSTM: 79.35 / 79.21 / 82.00 / 76.74 / 2.64 / 38.9 / 53.3. ResNet34 + ViT, 1 frame: 82.53 / 81.30 / 88.58 / 75.19 / 2.95 / 40.3 / 30.8. The paper says the standalone CNN and CNN + LSTM 'perform poorly' and adding the ViT 'significantly improves performance with little impact to inference speed'. My reading of the table, not a claim in the paper: adding the ViT raised precision by about 7 points over ResNet34 alone, while adding the 2-frame LSTM raised it by about 0.4 points; no spread is reported, so small differences cannot be judged.

Temporal alternatives, same population: ResNet34 + Transformer + ViT: 82.74 / 81.39 / 90.69 / 73.95 / 3.18 (58.9M, 50.6 ms). ResNet34 + ResNet18-3D: 83.10 / 82.26 / 88.91 / 76.65 / 2.87 (38.0M, 57.5 ms). The paper says all three alternate temporal architectures perform slightly worse than SmokeyNet.

Background subtraction, same population: MobileNet + LSTM + ViT: 81.79 / 80.71 / 88.34 / 74.31 / 3.92 (36.6M, 28.3 ms). The same model with a MOG2 channel: 83.12 / 82.65 / 88.79 / 77.43 / 3.72 (57.3M, 55.5 ms). The paper summarizes this as improving performance by almost 2%, mainly by improving recall by over 3%, while maintaining high precision, at the cost of model size and inference time.

Other backbones, same population: MobileNetFPN + LSTM + ViT: 80.58 / 80.68 / 82.36 / 79.12 / 2.43 (40.4M, 32.5 ms). EfficientNetB0 + LSTM + ViT: 82.55 / 81.68 / 88.45 / 75.89 / 3.56 (52.3M, 67.9 ms). TinyDeiT + LSTM + ViT: 79.74 / 79.01 / 84.25 / 74.44 / 3.61 (22.9M, 45.6 ms).

Standard baselines, 1 frame, same population: ResNet50: A 68.51, F1 74.30, P 63.35, R 89.89, TTD 1.01 min. FasterRCNN: 71.56 / 66.92 / 81.34 / 56.88 / 5.01. MaskRCNN: 73.24 / 69.94 / 81.08 / 61.51 / 4.18. The authors say ResNet50 is the fastest to detect a fire but 'only accomplishes this by generating an unacceptable amount of false positives'. A low TTD on its own does not show a good detector.

Human baseline: 3 lab members, 62 images (one random image per test fire, each shown with its previous frame). Average accuracy 78.5% (sigma 1.52%), F1 82.8% (sigma 0.73%), precision 93.5% (sigma 4.66%), recall 74.4% (sigma 1.90%). The model figures the paper compares against match the Table 2 full test-set figures; the paper does not report the model on the same 62 images, so the comparison is not on identical images.

Counterfactual, not measured: 'If the false positives derived from low-altitude clouds could be corrected, SmokeyNet would achieve 85.8% accuracy and 94.8% precision'. This is a hypothetical recomputation and no model achieved it.

Dataset counts: 315 sequences, 24,800 images, 101 cameras, 30 stations. Split: train 144 fires (11.3K images), validation 64 (4.9K), test 62 (4.9K), omitted 45 (3.7K). Annotation gaps: 1,213 positive images missing contour masks (280 because smoke is hard to see, 486 with boxes only, 447 randomly spread). 727 positive images were excluded from training.

Secondhand, reported by these authors about Govil et al. (2020) and not measured here: test accuracy 0.91 and F1 0.89 on 250 hand-selected images from the same video sequences as training (training set about 8,500 images). In a field test on 65 HPWREN cameras over nine days in October 2019, after suppressing repeat detections in a one-hour timespan, only 21% of notifications showed smoke from real fires (the paper calls this a 79% false positive rate; strictly it is a false discovery share of notifications), and there was no report of how many actual fires were missed.

My own analysis of the authors' published split lists, not a paper result: 10 of 62 test sequences share a date-plus-name key with a train sequence. 1 of these is a named event (20200601_WILDLAND-DRILLS, 4 train cameras and 1 test camera); the other 9 use the generic 'FIRE' name and may be different fires on the same date. 46 of 62 test sequences come from a camera string that also has a train sequence. 17 of 20 test station prefixes appear in train. All 5 named events shared by validation and test: 20200806 SpringsFire, 20200822 SloaneFire, 20200828 BorderFire, 20200905 ValleyFire, 20201216 ChaparralFire. 21 generic date-plus-'FIRE' keys span splits.
must_not_transfer: Smoke as proof of embers. FIgLib labels are whether smoke is visible in a remote mountaintop fixed-camera scene, at about 1 frame per minute. The paper neither labels nor discusses embers (its only finer annotations are smoke boxes and masks for the 144 train fires). Nothing in this paper links smoke presence to ember presence, count or position, so smoke must not count as evidence that a candidate is an ember.

A mandatory smoke gate. The paper gives no evidence that requiring smoke improves ember precision. Design reasoning, not from the source: visible embers can occur without visible smoke in frame, and smoke occurs without embers, so a gate would add a second error source with unknown recall and could silently drop true ember tracks. Smoke may at most be an optional context feature that has to win an ablation.

Any SmokeyNet number as a target or baseline for wfglink: 83.49% accuracy, 89.84% precision, 76.45% recall, 82.59% F1, 3.12 min TTD. These are image-level smoke classifications on a FIgLib test split drawn from a roughly balanced dataset. They are not track-level, not ember-level and not count-level, and do not reflect real-world prevalence.

Precision values in general. The paper itself warns that the 50/50 balance is not representative of real-world scenarios and may induce a higher false positive rate on real-world data. Precision measured on a balanced set says nothing about precision at wfglink's real candidate prevalence.

The claim that FIgLib's splitting by fires ensures 'no data related to the test set are in the training set'. The published lists show the split unit is a camera sequence. The same named event appears in train and test from different cameras, most test cameras and stations also appear in train, and validation and test share 5 named fires. The split is neither camera-disjoint nor site-disjoint, and not strictly event-disjoint. wfglink should not copy this grouping key as if it prevented leakage.

The temporal design and its ablation conclusions. SmokeyNet's temporal context is 2 or 3 frames about 60 s apart, which captures plume growth. wfglink candidates are tracked at video frame rate over far shorter time scales (a wfglink-side fact, not from this source), so the paper's finding that a third frame only marginally improves performance, and the Table 2 pattern that the LSTM adds about 1 accuracy point over ResNet34 + ViT, do not carry over to ember trajectories.

The Table 2 pattern that adding the ViT gave the largest precision gain in the ablation (my reading of the table; the paper says it 'significantly improves performance'). That concerns amorphous smoke spread across 45 large tiles. It has not been shown for small point-like ember candidates.

Tuned constants: 224 px tiles with 20 px overlap, 45 tiles, a 250-pixel tile label threshold, positive weights 5 and 40, resize to 1392x1856, and a crop of the top 352 rows. These depend on FIgLib resolution, horizon geometry and class ratios.

Positive-class upweighting as a default. The paper describes raising the image positive weight as trading precision for higher recall, and chose 5 for balanced precision and recall and better accuracy and F1. Recall-leaning upweighting runs against wfglink's precision-first goal.

FIgLib's negative taxonomy (clouds, fog, haze, glare, smog) as a complete list of ember confusers. Ember false positives come from different sources (specular glints, artificial lights, non-wildfire sparks, insects, hot pixels, compression flicker, sunlit leaves; wfglink-side list, not from the source). Clouds and fog matter mostly as background.

FIgLib images or labels as training data for the ember patch or temporal classifier. The frame rate is about 1 per minute, the scenes are wide mountaintop views, and the labels are smoke-only, so neither ember positives nor useful temporal negatives for ember tracks exist there.

The human-parity claim ('rivals human performance'). The human baseline used 62 images and 3 lab members, and the model's figures come from the full test set. It says nothing about human or model ember counting.
The counterfactual 85.8% accuracy and 94.8% precision. It is hypothetical, not a measured result.

The Govil et al. field-test figure (21% of notifications showed smoke from real fires after 1-hour suppression). It is a secondhand report on a different system, cameras and protocol, and is not a calibration target.
Runtime and model size (56.9M params, 51.6 ms/image, measurement hardware not stated). These do not represent wfglink's target hardware or a small patch classifier.
proposed_adaptations: Proposed adaptation: group splits by physical event and recording session, not by clip file or camera view. Keep every clip and view of the same burn or recording in a single split. Store the split lists as versioned files, as FIgLib published its lists. Normalize names before checking (FIgLib's own list has one malformed name that hides a shared key). Run an automatic overlap check (event, session, camera, location, date) that fails the build if keys are shared between splits. Report any camera or site overlap that remains, rather than claiming the split is leakage-free.

Proposed adaptation: seal the test set and keep validation and test event-disjoint too. Use validation only for early stopping, threshold choice and calibration. FIgLib's validation and test share named fires, and FIgLib selects the model by lowest validation loss, so information can leak through model selection.

Proposed adaptation: if hard negatives are mined from held-out data, split the held-out pool and leave one part untouched as the sealed test. This follows the procedure the authors propose (but did not carry out) in Section 7.4.

Proposed adaptation: make accepted-track precision the primary metric, defined exactly (an accepted track counts as TP if matched to a labeled ember track under a stated matching rule). Report recall, F1 and count error next to it. Always state the positive prevalence of the evaluation set. Also report false accepts per minute of ember-free video, because balanced evaluation inflates precision.

Proposed adaptation: define a causal time-to-accept for each true ember track, in frames and ms from track birth to verifier acceptance, with the time origin stated. Report never-accepted tracks separately as misses instead of leaving their handling unstated, as FIgLib's TTD does. Always pair it with false accepts per minute, because the FIgLib authors attribute ResNet50's fastest TTD to an unacceptable amount of false positives.

Proposed adaptation: make labels offline with full past and future context, but evaluate the verifier strictly causally. Report early-track performance (the first N frames after birth) separately, since FIgLib reports that early, faint smoke is hard under limited causal context (human baseline) and is a common miss (Figure 3 caption).

Proposed adaptation: build an ablation table modeled on Table 2. Rows: rules only; single-patch classifier; patch plus short causal frame stack; patch plus track-feature sequence; optional background-subtraction channel; optional context window around the patch. Use the same grouped splits for every row, average several runs (FIgLib averaged five), report the spread across runs (FIgLib did not), and report params and ms per candidate with the hardware stated.

Proposed adaptation: test a background-subtraction or frame-difference channel as an optional input to the patch classifier. In FIgLib, MOG2 mainly raised recall at higher size and time cost. Keep it only if it raises precision or recall at a fixed precision on validation.

Proposed adaptation: do not raise frame-level or clip-level alarms by OR over candidates; decide per track and count only accepted tracks. FIgLib reports that the any-tile-positive rule did worse for tile-to-image aggregation in non-ViT baselines, but gives no numbers, so this is weak supporting evidence, not a measured result for tracks.

Proposed adaptation: create a labeled hard-negative set with ember-specific categories (glints, lights, non-wildfire sparks, insects, hot pixels, compression flicker, bright foliage) and report the false accept rate per category. Include same-scene clips from before embers appear, analogous to FIgLib's 40 min of pre-ignition frames, so negatives share background with positives.

Proposed adaptation: for precision-first operation, do not upweight positives by default. Choose the acceptance threshold on validation to meet a stated target precision, then report recall at that operating point on the sealed test.

Proposed adaptation: add a per-clip timeline plot of accepted and rejected tracks over time, colored by correct or incorrect (modeled on Figure 3). Use it for error audits, and name systematic false positive and miss categories (for example occlusion, faint start, fade-out), as Section 6.2 does.

Proposed adaptation: a static region-of-interest mask (for example sky, or known fixed bright sources) is allowed only if it is fixed per clip before any test results are seen, documented, and judged on validation. This is the analog of FIgLib's horizon crop, without its constants.

Proposed adaptation: if smoke or haze cues are ever used, make them an optional non-gating feature that must show a validation gain in the ablation table. Never make a smoke check a required stage before counting.

problems.claim: relevant_methods[2] (own check): '7 named events span more than one split, 6 of them validation and test (for example SpringsFire, SloaneFire, ValleyFire, ChaparralFire).'
problems.issue: Miscount. Re-running the overlap on the published lists gives 7 named date-plus-name events across splits, but only 5 of them span validation and test. The other two are train plus test and train plus validation. This also contradicts the record's own results item, which lists exactly 5 shared validation and test events.
problems.correction: 7 named events span splits: 5 span validation and test (20200806 SpringsFire, 20200822 SloaneFire, 20200828 BorderFire, 20200905 ValleyFire, 20201216 ChaparralFire), 1 spans train and test (20200601 WILDLAND-DRILLS) and 1 spans train and validation (20190803 OtaySouth).

problems.claim: relevant_methods[2]: '20 more date-plus-generic-FIRE keys span splits'
problems.issue: The count depends on parsing. The train list has one malformed name, 20190825_FIRE-smer-tcs8-mobo-c (a hyphen where the other names have an underscore). Parsed as date 20190825, name FIRE, it shares a key with validation 20190825_FIRE_sm-w-mobo-c, which makes the count 21. Three of these keys (20190826, 20191003, 20191006) span all three splits.

problems.claim: reported_results[0]: 'Timing on one NVIDIA 2080Ti (Section 5.2)'; must_not_transfer: '51.6 ms/image on a 2080Ti'
problems.issue: Over-claim. Section 5.2 only says models were trained on a single NVIDIA 2080Ti. The paper gives no hardware, batch size or measurement setup for the inference times in Table 2.
problems.correction: Say that the paper does not state the hardware used to measure inference time (ms/image), and that a single 2080Ti is named for training only.

problems.claim: relevant_methods[0]: 'Frames before the start are labeled no-smoke and frames after are labeled smoke.'
problems.issue: Oversimplified label definition. Section 3.1 says only that the images from 40 min before and after the start of the fire serve as binary smoke/no-smoke labels. Section 6.3 says the ground truth was made by a human expert with full past and future context to precisely determine the first frame in which smoke is visible. So the positive onset is that expert-judged frame, not a separately known ignition time.
problems.correction: Labels are binary per image. The positive onset is the first frame in which smoke is visible, as judged by an expert with full temporal context (Section 6.3).

problems.claim: relevant_methods[2]: 'Train = 144 fires with bounding box or contour annotations'
problems.issue: The paper says the smoke in 144 fires 'has been manually annotated with bounding boxes and contour masks' (and, not or). Section 4.1 adds that some positive images inside those fires lack masks.
problems.correction: Train = the 144 fires annotated with bounding boxes and contour masks (53.3% of eligible fires, 11,300 images). Some positive images in them lack masks.

problems.claim: relevant_methods[7]: the paper says raising this weight 'trade[s] off precision for higher recall'; must_not_transfer: 'The authors upweight positives to favor recall.'
problems.issue: The quote was altered. The verbatim text is 'to trade off precision for higher recall'. The record also leaves out the stated reason for picking 5: 'to achieve more balanced precision and recall and improve the overall accuracy and F1-score'. Saying the authors upweight 'to favor recall' is only half of what the paper says.
problems.correction: Quote 'to trade off precision for higher recall' exactly, and add the reason for the value 5 as a verbatim quote. In must_not_transfer, say that the paper presents upweighting as trading precision for recall and chose 5 for balance, and that this recall lean runs against precision-first.

problems.claim: relevant_methods[9]: 'Pre-ignition false positives do not enter TTD.'
problems.issue: This is stated as fact but is the record's own inference from the definition. The paper also does not state the time origin of TTD or how TTD is combined across the five runs.
problems.correction: Mark it as the record's own reading. Add that the time origin, the handling of never-detected fires and the cross-run averaging of TTD are not stated.

problems.claim: reported_results[0]: 'FIgLib test split (62 fire sequences, about 4.9K images, roughly balanced)'
problems.issue: Section 7.2 states the 50/50 balance for the whole dataset. The class balance of the test split is not reported.
problems.correction: Say the paper states the whole dataset is roughly 50/50 but does not report the test split's class balance.

problems.claim: must_not_transfer (precision): 'The paper itself warns that ... real-world false positive rates will be higher.'
problems.issue: Overstated. The paper says the balance 'may induce models to incur a higher false positive rate on real-world data'.
problems.correction: Replace 'will be higher' with the paper's hedged 'may induce a higher false positive rate on real-world data'.

problems.claim: must_not_transfer (temporal): the findings that 'LSTM adds little' or 'a third frame is marginal'
problems.issue: These are written as quotes but are not in the paper. The paper says the standalone CNN and CNN + LSTM 'perform poorly', and that one additional frame 'only marginally improves performance at the cost of a 55.6% increase in inference time'. 'LSTM adds little' is the record's reading of Table 2. Also, 'Ember tracks live over tens of milliseconds' is a wfglink-side assumption that does not come from this source and is stated too narrowly.
problems.correction: Use the verbatim paper wording. Label the LSTM point as the record's reading of Table 2 (about 1 accuracy point over ResNet34 + ViT). Mark the ember time scale as a wfglink-side fact, not from the source.

problems.claim: must_not_transfer (smoke): 'seen kilometers away' and 'No ember is resolvable or labeled'; FIgLib-as-training item: 'the scenes are far away'
problems.issue: Not in the source. The paper says only 'remote mountain tops' and gives no viewing distance. It never discusses whether embers can be resolved.
problems.correction: Say: remote mountaintop fixed-camera scenes, at about 1 frame per minute. The paper neither labels nor discusses embers.

problems.claim: must_not_transfer: FIgLib's 'split by fires'; proposed_adaptations: FIgLib found 'any tile positive' worse
problems.issue: Pseudo-quotes. The paper says 'Splitting the data by fires' and describes the rule as 'if the prediction for any tile is positive for smoke, the full image is also classified as positive'. The tile-OR finding is also unquantified ('resulted in worse performance'). It applies only to tile-to-image aggregation in non-ViT baselines, so it is weak support for a track-level design rule.
problems.correction: Quote the exact wording. In the OR adaptation, add that the paper gives no numbers and that this is weak supporting evidence, not a measured result for tracks.

problems.claim: relevant_methods[12]: 'the holdout would have to be split in two with one half left untouched'; proposed_adaptations: 'This follows the authors' own rule in Section 7.4.'
problems.issue: The paper says to 'split our holdout set in two and leave one untouched'. It does not say the parts are equal halves. The procedure is proposed future work, not a rule the authors applied.
problems.correction: Write 'one part left untouched (relative sizes not stated)', and 'follows the procedure the authors propose (but did not carry out) in Section 7.4'.

problems.issue: The paper says 'an average over five runs'. Seeds are not mentioned. The record also does not say that Table 2 reports no spread for any model, which matters when small differences are read as findings (for example 83.49 vs 83.62).

relevant_methods.method: Problem framing: class imbalance and classic bootstrapping (hard negative mining)
relevant_methods.details: Detection reduced to classification creates a large imbalance between object and background examples. The paper says this can be as extreme as 100,000 background examples to every one object for sliding-window detectors such as DPM, and may still be high (e.g. 70:1) for proposal-based detectors. It names two classic mining algorithms. (1) For SVMs: keep a working set, train to convergence, remove easy examples (correctly classified beyond the margin), add hard ones (margin violators); this leads to the global SVM solution. (2) For non-SVM models: train on positives plus random negatives, run the model on a larger set to harvest false positives, add them, and retrain; this is usually iterated once and has no convergence proof. Both follow an alternation template: a fixed model finds examples, then the model trains on a fixed active set. The paper argues that freezing a deep ConvNet trained with SGD over hundreds of thousands of steps, even for a few iterations at a time, would dramatically slow progress, so a purely online form is needed.
relevant_methods.location: Section 1 (p.1 to 2); Section 2, paragraph 'Hard example mining' (p.2)

relevant_methods.method: Baseline heuristic minibatch sampling in Fast R-CNN (FRCN)
relevant_methods.details: Each SGD minibatch samples N images and then B/N RoIs per image, with N=2 and B=128. The per-RoI loss is a classification log loss plus a localization loss. Foreground: IoU with ground truth of at least 0.5. Background: maximum IoU with ground truth in [bg_lo, 0.5), with bg_lo=0.1 (used by FRCN and SPPnet). The paper says this bg_lo rule 'is hypothesized in [14] to crudely approximate hard negative mining', on the assumption that partly overlapping regions are the confusing ones. Foreground to background is rebalanced to 1:3 (25% foreground) by randomly undersampling background. The authors state that removing this ratio (random sampling) or increasing it lowers FRCN accuracy by about 3 points mAP (no table given).
relevant_methods.location: Section 3.1 'Training', paragraphs 'Foreground RoIs', 'Background RoIs', 'Balancing fg-bg RoIs' (p.3)

relevant_methods.method: Online hard example mining (OHEM): loss-based selection inside each minibatch
relevant_methods.details: At SGD iteration t, compute the conv feature map for each image. Run the RoI network forward on ALL input RoIs R (Figure 2 labels the selective search RoIs of an image as |R| about 2000; Section 4.2 says N=2 gives |R| about 4000), not on a sampled subset. Compute each RoI's loss (classification plus bbox regression) under the current network, sort the RoIs by loss, and keep the hardest. Section 4.1 phrases this per input image as 'taking the B/N examples'; Section 4.2 says all RoIs from all N images are used as R, and the Figure 2 caption says the module selects B examples (B=128). The paper does not spell out whether the top-K cut is applied per image or over the pooled R. Only the selected RoIs go through forward and backward passes. The model is in effect frozen for exactly one minibatch, so it updates as often as baseline SGD. The extra forward cost is 'relatively small' because computation is shared through the conv feature map. The backward pass is 'no more expensive than before', because only the selected RoIs are backpropagated. The Introduction describes the selection as sampling from a non-uniform, non-stationary distribution that depends on the current loss and favors diverse, high-loss instances.

relevant_methods.method: NMS deduplication among candidate RoIs, ranked by loss
relevant_methods.details: Co-located RoIs with high overlap are likely to have correlated losses. They can also project onto the same region of the conv feature map because of resolution disparity, which leads to loss double counting. Standard NMS (the FRCN implementation) is applied with loss as the score: repeatedly take the RoI with the highest loss, then remove lower-loss RoIs that overlap it heavily. A relaxed IoU threshold of 0.7 suppresses only highly overlapping RoIs. The Figure 2 diagram labels the selection module 'Diverse & Hard RoI Sampler'; the caption calls it the 'Hard RoI module'.

relevant_methods.method: Removal of the bg_lo threshold and the fg-bg ratio
relevant_methods.details: OHEM uses bg_lo=0 (Table 1 rows 11 to 13) and no fixed foreground to background ratio. The argument: if a class were neglected, its loss would rise until it is likely to be sampled. A minibatch may be all background when foreground is easy (e.g. a canonical view of a car), or all foreground when background is trivial (sky, grass).

relevant_methods.method: Implementation: read-only RoI network versus loss masking
relevant_methods.details: Option 1: compute loss for all RoIs in the loss layer, sort, and set non-hard losses to 0. This is straightforward but inefficient, because memory is still allocated and a backward pass is run for every RoI. Option 2 (used): keep two copies of the RoI network with shared weights (Figure 2 legend). The read-only copy runs forward only on all RoIs; the hard RoI sampling module selects R_hard-sel; the regular copy runs forward and backward only on R_hard-sel, accumulates the gradients and passes them to the conv network. Implemented in Caffe with gradient accumulation over N single-image forward-backward passes. With N=2, |R| about 4000 and B=128, the authors report option 2 has a similar memory footprint to option 1 but is more than 2 times faster.

Two backbones: VGG_CNN_M_1024 (VGGM, a wider version of AlexNet) and VGG16. Train on PASCAL VOC 2007 trainval and test on VOC 2007 test. SGD for 80k iterations, initial LR 0.001, decayed by 0.1 every 30k iterations. Baselines (Table 1 rows 1 and 2) were reproduced on this schedule and are slightly higher than in the original FRCN paper. The paper reports one number per configuration and says nothing about seeds, repeated runs or variance.

relevant_methods.method: Controlled comparisons: OHEM versus heuristic sampling versus using all RoIs
relevant_methods.details: Conditions: FRCN with bg_lo=0.1 versus bg_lo=0. N=1 versus N=2 images per batch, run 'in order to increase correlation in an effort to break our method'. Standard FRCN with a large minibatch B=2048, bg_lo=0 and N in {1,2}, with LR retuned to 0.003 (VGG16) and 0.004 (VGGM), as the 'train with all the RoIs and let easy ones contribute little gradient' alternative. OHEM with B=128 and bg_lo=0. Results are in Table 1.

To compare methods fairly regardless of how each samples examples, model snapshots taken every 20k steps are run over the entire VOC07 trainval set, and the average loss per RoI over all RoIs is reported for the VGG16 variants (Figure 3). Figure 3 has two panels: one for N=2 runs (FRCN, FRCN bg_lo=0, FRCN bg_lo=0 B=2048, Our Approach bg_lo=0) and one for the corresponding N=1 runs.

relevant_methods.method: Explanation of why OHEM beats heuristic sampling (as argued in the paper)
relevant_methods.details: (a) The bg_lo heuristic 'helps convergence and detection accuracy' but is suboptimal because it ignores some infrequent but important difficult background regions. (b) The 1:3 ratio is a hyperparameter that the authors say OHEM can remove 'with no ill effect', because a neglected class's loss rises until it is sampled, so the mix of foreground and background in a minibatch can follow what is currently hard in each image (my paraphrase of Sections 3.1 and 4.1). (c) Selection happens every iteration with the current model, so 'learning is not delayed'. (d) Empirically, OHEM reaches the lowest full-set training loss (Figure 3) and the highest test mAP in Table 1, and beats the use-all-RoIs variant. The authors also say OHEM trains faster than the use-all-RoIs variant because it computes gradients with a smaller minibatch, but they report no timing for the B=2048 runs. The paper gives empirical support but no formal analysis of why use-all-RoIs underperforms.
relevant_methods.location: Section 3.1 (p.3); Section 4 opening and 4.1 (p.4); Sections 5.2 to 5.5 (p.5 to 6)

relevant_methods.details: Seconds per training iteration and maximum memory on one Nvidia Titan X GPU, for FRCN and OHEM with VGGM and VGG16. Some VGG16 settings use gradient accumulation over two forward/backward passes.

VGG16 on VOC07, VOC12 and MS COCO test-dev 2015. Schedules: VOC07 trainval uses the Section 5 schedule; 200k iterations with LR step 40k for the extra-data VOC sets (07+12 and 07++12); 240k iterations with step 160k for COCO. Additions: multi-scale training and testing (M; train s in {480,576,688,864,900}, test s in {480,576,688,864,1000}, max side capped at 1000, chosen because of GPU memory constraints) and iterative bbox regression with weighted voting (B; NMS at IoU 0.3, voting with boxes at IoU of at least 0.5). Table 6 ablates M (train and test separately) and B with and without OHEM.

relevant_methods.method: Concurrent loss-based selection works cited (not studied in this paper)
relevant_methods.details: [27] Simo-Serra et al. independently select hard positive and negative examples from a larger set of random examples based on their loss, to learn image descriptors. [33] Wang and Gupta, given a positive pair of patches, find hard negative patches from a large set using a triplet loss. [22] Loshchilov and Hutter investigate online loss-based selection of hard examples for minibatch SGD, focused on ConvNets for image classification. The paper only names these and gives no results for them.
relevant_methods.location: Section 2, paragraph 'Hard example selection in deep learning' (p.2)

Not reported anywhere in the paper: precision at a fixed operating point, false positive rates, calibration, per-image or per-video counts, any video or temporal results, any comparison against classic offline bootstrapping, any analysis of label noise, and any seeds, repeated runs, variance or confidence intervals. All accuracy numbers are single-run mAP or AP on still-image benchmarks.
must_not_transfer: None of the mAP or AP gains (for example +2.7 mAP on VOC07 with VGG16, or +2.9 AP on COCO) may be cited as an expected improvement for wfglink. They come from 2016 Fast R-CNN with VGG backbones and selective search proposals on PASCAL VOC and MS COCO still images. The paper has no ember, fire, night, glow, video or single-camera RGB streaming data.

mAP and AP summarize ranking quality over all detections, averaged over classes, and for COCO also over recall and IoU levels. They are not precision at a chosen threshold, false accepted tracks per minute, or count error. The paper does not show that OHEM raises precision at a high-confidence operating point, which is what a precision-first verifier needs.

Every number is a single reported value with no seeds, repeats or variance. Differences of about 1 point or less (VGG16 bg_lo 67.2 versus 67.5, OHEM N=1 69.7 versus N=2 69.9, FRCN N=1 66.3 versus 66.3) cannot be separated from run-to-run noise using this paper, so they must not be cited as established effects or non-effects.

The specific hyperparameters were tuned for FRCN on VOC and COCO: B=128, N=2, about 2000 RoIs per image, NMS IoU 0.7 on loss, bg_lo=0.1, the 1:3 ratio, and the learning rate schedules. They must not be carried over as validated settings for a small ember patch classifier or a temporal classifier.

The claim that OHEM removes the need for foreground to background balancing rests on thousands of candidates per image on VOC and COCO, where foreground RoIs are available in most images (the latter is my inference, not a statement in the paper). Rare-positive regimes and small candidate pools were not tested. wfglink must not drop class balancing or a positive quota without its own ablation.

The paper's statement that OHEM 'is helpful when dealing with smaller sized objects' is inferred from a +4.9 AP gain on COCO medium objects. Small-object AP only went from 3.5 to 5.0. Nothing in the paper concerns few-pixel point-like bright blobs, so it must not be cited as evidence that OHEM helps tiny ember candidates.

The claim that effectiveness grows as datasets become larger and harder rests on VOC versus COCO comparisons. It says nothing about small student datasets of a few clips and must not be used to predict wfglink behaviour.

Gains were not uniform across classes; some VOC07 classes got worse (aeroplane 74.6 to 71.2, sofa 68.7 to 66.2). Do not assume OHEM will improve rejection of every distractor type (headlights, reflections, sparks, lamps) evenly.

The N=1 result covers correlation among RoIs within one still image, and the authors' own conclusion frames it as robustness when fewer images per batch are needed to save GPU memory. It is not evidence of robustness to frame-to-frame near-duplicates in video or to many patches from one track. Do not cite it for temporal correlation.

The paper does not discuss label noise. Selecting the highest-loss examples may preferentially pick mislabeled or ambiguous patches, and the paper provides no evidence either way. Do not claim OHEM is robust to noisy ember labels.

The case for online over offline mining is the cost of freezing a deep ConvNet across hundreds of thousands of SGD steps. The paper does not compare OHEM to classic offline bootstrapping. Do not claim online mining is shown to beat periodic offline hard-negative mining for a tiny, cheap-to-retrain classifier.

The Table 2 timing and memory figures (Titan X, VGGM and VGG16), the 'more than 2 times faster' implementation claim and the unmeasured 'training is faster' claim versus B=2048 do not transfer to a small patch classifier or to runtime on a booth laptop. OHEM is described as a modification of SGD training, so by construction it should not change inference (my inference; the paper does not state inference cost), and the paper says nothing about inference-time verification latency.

OHEM is a training-time sampling method. It provides no inference-time acceptance rule, threshold, calibration, temporal reasoning, tracking, or causal decision logic. It cannot justify any design choice in the rules stage or in track acceptance by itself.

The finding that the bg_lo heuristic is suboptimal is specific to IoU-based background sampling in FRCN, and even there VGG16 was roughly unchanged without it (67.2 versus 67.5). Do not generalize it to 'all hand-made sampling heuristics hurt'. The 2016 state-of-the-art claims (78.9 and 76.3 mAP) also depend on multi-scale and iterative bbox regression and are irrelevant to wfglink.
proposed_adaptations: Proposed adaptation (loss-ranked selection over the candidate pool): at each training step of the small patch classifier, sample a few training clips or frames, take ALL candidates the existing blob detector produced in them as the pool (the analogue of RoIs), run the classifier forward without gradients, compute per-candidate classification loss with no reduction, and backpropagate only the top-K highest-loss candidates. Decide and document whether top-K is taken per frame or over the pooled candidates, since the paper is not explicit. Because the model is tiny, the simple loss-masking implementation (paper option 1) is likely adequate; the two-copy trick is probably not needed (untested judgment).

Proposed adaptation (spatial plus temporal deduplication): before taking the top K, apply loss-ranked NMS among candidates that overlap in the same frame, as the paper does with IoU 0.7 (the threshold must be retuned for small blobs). Add a temporal step the paper does not have: allow at most one or a few patches per track per short time window, because consecutive frames of one blob are near-duplicates and would double count loss, the same concern the paper raises for overlapping RoIs.

Proposed adaptation (hybrid sampling with a positive floor): since ember positives may be rare and the paper never tested extreme rarity, keep a minimum quota of labelled ember positives and a small random slice of easy negatives in each minibatch, plus the hard-selected examples. Ablate this against pure OHEM (no ratio) and against a fixed-ratio random sampler before choosing.

Proposed adaptation (add classic offline bootstrapping for precision): because retraining a tiny classifier is cheap, also run the verifier periodically over negative-only training footage (bright non-ember scenes such as lamps, headlights, reflections, glints) and add its accepted false positives to a persistent hard-negative bank sampled in later epochs. This is the Sung and Poggio style bootstrapping the paper describes in Section 1 (and the non-SVM variant in Section 2). It suits a precision-first goal. The paper did not compare the two approaches, so wfglink should test both.

Proposed adaptation (leakage control): mine hard examples only from training videos, never from validation or sealed test videos. Split by video or recording event, not by frame, so mined near-duplicates cannot leak across splits.

Proposed adaptation (sampling-independent monitoring, mirroring Section 5.5): evaluate each checkpoint on the full candidate set of a fixed validation split. Report mean loss per candidate together with precision-first metrics such as precision at a fixed recall and false accepted tracks per minute, so that methods with different samplers are compared fairly.

Proposed adaptation (ablation design mirroring Table 1): compare (a) random sampling with a fixed class ratio, (b) a heuristic hard-negative sampler, for example candidates near the ember brightness or color thresholds, as the analogue of bg_lo, (c) loss-ranked OHEM with dedup, and (d) training on all candidates with a retuned learning rate. Use the same schedule, several seeds, and held-out videos, and report confidence intervals rather than single numbers (the paper itself reports only single runs).

Proposed adaptation (label-noise guard, not from the paper): log the top-loss candidates every epoch for human audit, cap how often any single candidate or track can be selected, and allow annotators to mark ambiguous patches so they are excluded from hard selection. This keeps loss-based mining from amplifying labelling errors.

Proposed adaptation (temporal classifier): apply the same loss-ranked selection at the level of track windows. Compute the loss per causal window of each track, select the hardest windows per minibatch, and deduplicate overlapping windows from the same track by temporal overlap, the analogue of IoU-based NMS.

Proposed adaptation (precision-weighted loss for ranking): rank by classification loss only, since the patch classifier has no box regression term (the paper's ranking loss includes bbox regression). If the verifier must be precision-first, consider weighting the loss on false accepts (negatives scored as ember) more heavily when ranking hardness, and treat this as a hyperparameter to validate, not something the paper supports.

If any class were neglected, its loss would increase until it has a high probability of being sampled.

problems.claim: Section 5.3 result: 'The authors read this as robustness to within-image correlation among the selected examples.'
problems.issue: Within-image correlation is why the authors ran the experiment ('in order to increase correlation in an effort to break our method'), but it is not their stated conclusion. The paper's stated conclusion is: 'This shows that OHEM is robust in case one needs fewer images per batch in order to reduce GPU memory usage.'
problems.correction: Say the experiment was meant to raise within-image correlation, and quote the authors' actual conclusion about fewer images per batch and GPU memory. Update the matching must_not_transfer item to match.

problems.claim: Related work: '[27] Simo-Serra et al. select hard positive and negative patch pairs by loss from a larger random set'
problems.issue: The text obtained says '[27] independently selects hard positive and negative example from a larger set of random examples based on their loss to learn image descriptors'. The phrase 'patch pairs' is not in the paper. It comes from outside knowledge of [27].
problems.correction: Use the paper's own wording: hard positive and negative examples chosen by loss from a larger set of random examples, to learn image descriptors. For [33], keep 'given a positive pair of patches, finds hard negative patches from a large set using triplet loss'.

problems.claim: Explanation item (b), under the label 'as argued in the paper': 'Random undersampling to a fixed ratio is a hand-set hyperparameter, while loss-based selection adapts per image and per iteration to whatever the current model gets wrong.'
problems.issue: The paper does not argue this. It is the extractor's own synthesis. What the paper says is that the ratio can be removed 'with no ill effect' (Section 3.1), that a neglected class's loss rises until it gets sampled, and that a minibatch can be all foreground or all background (Section 4.1). Item (d) also repeats 'while training faster' as if measured, but no timing for the B=2048 runs is reported.
problems.correction: Restate (b) using the paper's own statements and mark the per-image adaptation wording as a paraphrase. In (d), say the 'training is faster' claim versus B=2048 is the authors' statement with no reported timing.

problems.claim: must_not_transfer: 'OHEM is training-only and adds no inference cost'
problems.issue: The paper never states the inference cost. This is a fair inference from the design (OHEM only changes SGD minibatch construction, and the inference description in Section 3 is unchanged), but the record presents it as fact from the paper.
problems.correction: Label it as the reviewer's inference: by construction it should not change inference, and the paper does not report inference cost.

problems.claim: Reported results and must_not_transfer do not mention run-to-run variance
problems.issue: It is missing. The paper reports one number per configuration and says nothing about seeds, repeated runs, variance or confidence intervals. Several conclusions rest on differences of under about 1 point: VGG16 bg_lo 67.2 versus 67.5 'remains roughly the same', OHEM N=1 at 69.7 versus N=2 at 69.9, and FRCN N=1 at 66.3 versus 66.3.
problems.correction: Add 'no seeds, repeated runs, variance or confidence intervals' to the not-reported list. Add a must_not_transfer item saying differences of about 1 point or less cannot be separated from noise using this paper.
